title: Explicit Construction Of The Normal Cone At Every Nonlocal Extreme Behaviour Of $\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$ And Device-independent Applications
authors: Yutian Wu, Xie Sicheng, Ravishankar Ramanathan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The set of quantum correlations [MATH], in the simplest Bell scenario with two parties performing two binary measurements each, is an object of fundamental interest both in quantum foundations and for device-independent applications. A nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in this set can maximize many different Bell expressions, yet these expressions are not all equally useful in a practical experiment. Here, firstly, we give an explicit characterization of every Bell expression maximized by any given nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in this Bell scenario. This determines the full normal cone at every such behaviour and makes it possible to optimize over all Bell tests with the same ideal behavior. We then derive an exact variational formula for the quantum bound of an arbitrary Bell expression in this scenario. As an example illustrating the construction, we derive the normal cone for a family of extremal quantum behaviours of importance in device-independent randomness certification, from Phys. Rev. Lett. 129, 150403, 2022. Finally, we explore the consequences of this characterization for device-independent randomness generation in practical experiments. Specifically, for any given detection efficiency [MATH], we construct Bell tests and two-qubit experiments that certify more single-round min-entropy from one Bell score than any CHSH score can certify with the same detector efficiency, even when the quantum devices used for the CHSH test are optimized. The results provide a systematic way to choose Bell tests for a desired quantum behaviour and to improve their performance for device-independent applications under experimental imperfections.
tldr: The paper explicitly characterizes the normal cone at every nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in the two-party two-binary-measurement Bell scenario and applies this to device-independent randomness certification.
motivation: Nonlocal extremal quantum behaviours can maximize many Bell expressions, but not all are equally useful in practical device-independent experiments. A systematic characterization of all Bell tests sharing the same ideal behaviour is needed to optimize DI protocols under experimental imperfections.
method: The authors construct the full normal cone at each nonlocal extremal behaviour of Q_2222, derive an exact variational formula for quantum Bell bounds, and illustrate the construction using extremal behaviours relevant to DI randomness certification.
result: They obtain explicit normal-cone descriptions, an exact variational formula for arbitrary Bell-expression quantum bounds, and construct Bell tests and two-qubit experiments that certify more single-round min-entropy than optimized CHSH tests at any given detection efficiency.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic framework for selecting Bell tests for a desired quantum behaviour and improving device-independent applications under realistic experimental conditions.

title: Frequency-bin-encoded Quantum Secret Sharing With Fast Basis Switching
authors: Chen-You Su, Suparna Seshadri, Hsuan-Hao Lu, Jason D. Mckinney, Andrew M. Weiner, Joseph M. Lukens
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frequency-bin encoding offers unique opportunities for fiber-native quantum information processing, yet its full potential has been hampered by challenges in rapid state control and protocol scaling. Leveraging high-speed microwave processing, we overcome several extant hurdles and unlock new fundamental capabilities in frequency-based quantum communications. First, we demonstrate three-party quantum secret sharing, representing, to our knowledge, the first multiparty ([MATH] users) quantum communication protocol implemented entirely with frequency encoding. Second, we demonstrate active, pseudorandom switching of frequency-bin quantum states and measurement bases at 20 MHz symbol rates, enabling real-time protocol operation without relying on hardware-intensive passive basis-selection schemes. Even under fast switching, we preserve high-contrast three-party correlations ([MATH]) and low quantum bit error rates ([MATH]). Our work extends frequency-bin quantum communication beyond static, two-party protocols, opening a pathway toward scalable, reconfigurable, and real-time spectrally encoded quantum networking.
tldr: Demonstrates the first fully frequency-bin-encoded three-party quantum secret sharing protocol with active 20 MHz basis switching, extending frequency-based quantum communication beyond static two-party schemes.
motivation: Frequency-bin encoding is attractive for fiber-native quantum information processing, but rapid state control and scaling to multiparty protocols have been major obstacles.
method: The authors use high-speed microwave processing to implement active pseudorandom switching of frequency-bin quantum states and measurement bases at 20 MHz symbol rates, and apply it to a three-party quantum secret sharing protocol.
result: They achieve high-contrast three-party correlations and low quantum bit error rates even under fast switching, enabling real-time protocol operation without passive hardware-intensive basis selection.
conclusion: This work establishes frequency-bin encoding as a viable platform for scalable, reconfigurable, real-time multiparty quantum networking and secret sharing.

title: Gravity-induced Entanglement Assisted By An Additional Interaction Using Magic Angle Calibration
authors: Daisuke Miki, Alfred Li, Yanbei Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gravity-induced entanglement provides an operational test of whether gravitational dynamics are compatible with local operations and classical communication (LOCC), but the weakness of the gravitational interaction and the presence of force noise make direct entanglement generation extremely demanding. We introduce a controllable additional coherent interaction that biases two test masses close to, but within, a separability-preservation bound, so that the weak Newtonian coupling supplies only the remaining coherent contribution needed for entanglement. If the additional interaction alone is shown to be incapable of generating entanglement, while entanglement is observed when gravity is included, the gravitational interaction provides a non-LOCC contribution. Since gravity cannot be turned off, we use a magic-angle null of the projected tidal coupling to calibrate the additional interaction and force noise. If the additional dynamics is certified to preserve separability at the magic angle and entanglement is subsequently observed in a non-null configuration, the gravitational contribution is incompatible with an LOCC description within the Markovian model. The protocol trades the stringent absolute force-noise requirement of direct schemes for precision in controlling the additional coupling, its backaction, and angle-dependent systematics.
tldr: The paper proposes a calibrated protocol to certify gravity-induced entanglement as a non-LOCC contribution by biasing two test masses near a separability-preservation bound with an additional coherent interaction.
motivation: Gravity-induced entanglement offers an operational test of whether gravity is compatible with LOCC, but direct entanglement generation is extremely demanding due to weak gravitational coupling and force noise.
method: An additional controllable coherent interaction is tuned so that it alone remains within a separability-preservation bound, while the weak Newtonian coupling supplies the remaining coherence needed for entanglement; a magic-angle null of the projected tidal coupling calibrates the additional interaction and force noise.
result: If separability is certified at the magic angle and entanglement is later observed in a non-null configuration, the gravitational contribution is incompatible with an LOCC description in the Markovian model, trading absolute force-noise requirements for precision in controlling the added coupling and systematics.
conclusion: The protocol provides a practical route to certify gravity-induced entanglement and non-LOCC gravitational dynamics using calibrated auxiliary interactions rather than ultra-low force noise alone.

title: Certification Of Non-stabilizerness In Multi-qubit Systems Via Worst-case Random Access Codes
authors: Santiago Zamora
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent works have proposed semi-device-independent frameworks to certify non-stabilizerness, but the complexity of the stabilizer polytope makes these methods infeasible beyond a few qubits. In this work, we address this limitation by moving to partially characterized measurements in the context of worst-case random access codes. We first establish a simple condition, which we term the stabilizer pigeonhole criterion, that certifies non-stabilizerness in [MATH]-qubit pure states, and show how it can be applied to reduced states. As an application, we certify magic in [MATH] states of arbitrary size using only eight preparations and three single-qubit measurement settings. Motivated by recent work on the stabilizer marginal problem, we then construct prepare-and-measure correlations generated by global [MATH]-qubit quantum states for which every [MATH]-qubit marginal lies inside the stabilizer polytope, yet the combined correlations cannot be reproduced by any global stabilizer mixture. Finally, we derive analytical upper and lower bounds on the worst-case bias attainable with mixed stabilizer preparations in an [MATH]-qubit random access code with [MATH] Pauli measurements. For the complete set of [MATH] non-identity Pauli measurements, we show that the optimal quantum and mixed-stabilizer biases both scale as [MATH], and that their ratio is asymptotically bounded by a constant ([MATH]), showing that in this setting, magic in the preparations alone yields at most a constant-factor advantage over stabilizer mixtures.
tldr: The paper introduces semi-device-independent methods to certify non-stabilizerness in multi-qubit systems using worst-case random access codes and a stabilizer pigeonhole criterion.
motivation: Certifying magic (non-stabilizerness) is a key resource-theoretic task, but existing semi-device-independent approaches are computationally infeasible beyond a few qubits due to the complexity of the stabilizer polytope.
method: The author develops a stabilizer pigeonhole criterion for certifying non-stabilizerness in pure and reduced states, constructs prepare-and-measure correlations from global quantum states with stabilizer marginals, and derives bounds on worst-case bias in random access codes with Pauli measurements.
result: Magic is certified for arbitrary-size states using only eight preparations and three single-qubit measurement settings, and the optimal quantum versus mixed-stabilizer bias ratio is shown to be asymptotically bounded by a constant for the complete set of non-identity Pauli measurements.
conclusion: The work provides scalable certification of non-stabilizerness and clarifies the limited advantage that magic in preparations can offer over stabilizer mixtures in certain random access code settings.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the challenge of certifying non-stabilizerness (magic) in quantum states without full device characterization. The authors introduce the stabilizer pigeonhole criterion, a simple condition that certifies magic in m-qubit pure states by leveraging the fact that the stabilizer polytope has a limited number of vertices. They show that this criterion can be applied to reduced states, enabling the certification of magic in W states of arbitrary size using only eight preparations and three single-qubit measurement settings. Motivated by the stabilizer marginal problem, they construct prepare-and-measure correlations from global m-qubit states where every k-qubit marginal lies inside the stabilizer polytope, yet the global correlations cannot be reproduced by any stabilizer mixture, demonstrating a form of non-local magic. Finally, they analyze worst-case random access codes with n Pauli measurements, deriving analytical bounds on the bias achievable with mixed stabilizer preparations. For the complete set of 4^m-1 non-identity Pauli measurements, they find that both optimal quantum and mixed-stabilizer biases scale as 2^{-3m/2}, with their ratio asymptotically bounded by a constant (≲1.85), indicating that magic in preparations alone yields at most a constant-factor advantage over stabilizer mixtures in this setting.

Demonstration that magic can be certified in W states of arbitrary size using only eight preparations and three single-qubit measurement settings.
Construction of prepare-and-measure correlations where all k-qubit marginals are stabilizer but the global correlations are not, highlighting the limitations of marginal-based certification.

Derivation of analytical upper and lower bounds on the worst-case bias in random access codes with mixed stabilizer preparations, showing scaling as 2^{-3m/2} and a constant-factor advantage (≲1.85) for quantum over stabilizer strategies.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors adopt a semi-device-independent approach, moving from fully characterized to partially characterized measurements to overcome the computational infeasibility of the stabilizer polytope for many qubits. The stabilizer pigeonhole criterion is based on a counting argument: if the number of possible measurement outcomes exceeds the number of stabilizer states, at least one outcome must be non-stabilizer. This is applied to reduced states by considering marginals. For the random access code analysis, they formulate the problem as a game where a sender encodes classical information into a quantum state and a receiver performs Pauli measurements to guess the input. They derive bounds on the worst-case bias using semidefinite programming and analytical techniques, comparing optimal quantum strategies with those restricted to stabilizer mixtures.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents several key results. First, the stabilizer pigeonhole criterion successfully certifies magic in W states for any number of qubits using a minimal set of measurements (eight preparations, three settings). Second, the constructed correlations show that even if all k-qubit marginals are within the stabilizer polytope, the global state can be non-stabilizer, proving that marginal-based certification is incomplete. Third, for random access codes with all 4^m-1 non-identity Pauli measurements, both the optimal quantum bias and the mixed-stabilizer bias scale as 2^{-3m/2}, with their ratio bounded by approximately 1.85. This indicates that the advantage of magic states over stabilizer mixtures is at most a constant factor, diminishing the perceived power of magic in this context.

Demonstrates practical certification with minimal resources (eight preparations, three settings) for W states of arbitrary size.

title: Generalized Wigner-Yanase Uncertainty Bounds For Multiple Quantum Channels
authors: Jianming Zhou, Xiaoli Hu, Naihuan Jing
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive uncertainty relations for quantum channels based on the generalized Wigner-Yanase skew information. For three channels, we obtain a product lower bound by optimizing over permutations of commutator and anticommutator pairings. For an arbitrary number of channels, we establish a lower bound on the sum of squared uncertainties and construct a hierarchy of bounds using the partial Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. These bounds are invariant under changes of Kraus representation for a fixed operator basis. The first two levels of the hierarchy coincide with the elementary arithmetic-geometric mean bound, while the intermediate levels generally depend on the ordering of the operator basis. Examples involving three and four qubit channels demonstrate the bounds and compare their performance with an earlier pairing inequality under fixed channel representations.
tldr: The paper derives generalized Wigner-Yanase skew-information uncertainty bounds for multiple quantum channels, including product bounds for three channels and a hierarchy of sum-squared uncertainty bounds for arbitrary numbers of channels.
motivation: Uncertainty relations are fundamental in quantum information, and the Wigner-Yanase skew information provides a way to quantify quantum uncertainty; extending such bounds from states to multiple quantum channels is a natural and technically relevant problem.
method: The authors optimize over commutator and anticommutator pairings to obtain a product lower bound for three channels, and use a partial Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to construct a hierarchy of lower bounds on the sum of squared uncertainties for arbitrarily many channels.
result: The bounds are invariant under changes of Kraus representation for a fixed operator basis; the first two hierarchy levels coincide with the arithmetic-geometric mean bound, while intermediate levels generally depend on operator-basis ordering, and examples with three and four qubit channels compare their performance to an earlier pairing inequality.
conclusion: This work provides a new family of channel-based uncertainty bounds using generalized Wigner-Yanase skew information, with representation-invariant properties and a hierarchical structure that may be useful for quantifying uncertainty in quantum channels.

title: Entropy Production From Crossing A Quantum Separatrix
authors: James R. Anglin Peter Stabel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: If the Hamiltonian of a large quantum system depends on a variable parameter, its parameter-dependent energy spectrum may often form a dense lattice of avoided crossings. If the parameter slowly changes, the system's time evolution through the avoided crossings tends in the semi-classical limit to change from adiabatic to diabatic across a narrow energy range that has recently been defined as a quantum separatrix. Here we show that in the extreme semi-classical limit of a quasi-continuously dense spectrum, all quantum separatrices form a universal one-parameter family, and that evolution through the separatrix becomes efficiently ergodizing. If the unitary evolution is realistically averaged over small variations in the parameter time dependence, quantum separatrix crossing generates diagonal entropy according to a universal formula. Numerical examples confirm that the results for quasi-continuous spectra remain clearly recognizable in finite systems, with only small finite-size effects.
tldr: The paper derives a universal entropy-production formula for quantum systems driven across a dense spectrum of avoided crossings, identifying a semi-classical 'quantum separatrix' transition that becomes ergodizing.
motivation: Slow parameter changes through dense avoided crossings are common in large quantum systems, but the resulting transition from adiabatic to diabatic dynamics and its thermodynamic consequences are not fully characterized.
method: The authors analyze the semi-classical limit of quasi-continuously dense spectra, show that quantum separatrices form a universal one-parameter family, and average unitary evolution over small parameter-timing variations.
result: Crossing the quantum separatrix efficiently ergodizes the system and generates diagonal entropy according to a universal formula, with numerical finite-system examples confirming only small finite-size corrections.
conclusion: Quantum separatrix crossing provides a generic mechanism for entropy production in driven large quantum systems, with universal predictions that should be observable in finite systems.

title: Thermalization And Quantum Chaos In A Pure Gauge Discrete non-Abelian Lattice Gauge Theory
authors: Marco Vaia, Edoardo Ballini, Alberto Bottarelli, Matteo M. Wauters, Philipp Hauke
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gauge theories constitute the basis of our microscopic description of fundamental physical laws, and they are a cornerstone of contemporary scientific research. Yet, how such systems thermalize far from equilibrium remains a fundamental open question at the crossroads of statistical, high-energy, and condensed-matter physics. In this work, we investigate the thermalization properties of non-Abelian lattice gauge theories, focusing on the discrete gauge group [MATH], which is ideally suited for current qudit-based quantum simulators. Specifically, we study a linear plaquette chain in a gauge-fixed formulation that removes unphysical degrees of freedom. A numerical analysis of the Hamiltonian spectrum and expectation values of local operators shows a behavior broadly aligned with the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH). We also study thermalization through the real-time dynamics of the entanglement spectrum, confirming the emergence of random-matrix level statistics after an initial transient. Our results expand the rich phenomenology of dihedral non-Abelian gauge systems. Once the relevant symmetry structure is properly resolved, the model displays the same qualitative ETH-based thermalization scenario observed in Abelian gauge models and generic non-integrable quantum many-body systems.

motivation: Understanding far-from-equilibrium thermalization of non-Abelian gauge theories is an open question at the intersection of statistical, high-energy, and condensed-matter physics, with relevance to qudit-based quantum simulators.
method: The authors analyze a gauge-fixed linear plaquette chain with a discrete non-Abelian gauge group, using Hamiltonian spectrum statistics, local operator expectation values, and real-time entanglement-spectrum dynamics.
result: They observe behavior broadly consistent with the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis and find that random-matrix level statistics emerge after an initial transient in the entanglement-spectrum dynamics.
conclusion: Once the relevant symmetry structure is resolved, the model exhibits the same qualitative ETH-based thermalization scenario as Abelian gauge models and generic non-integrable quantum many-body systems, expanding the phenomenology of dihedral non-Abelian gauge systems.

title: Resonance-controlled Post-selected Mode Entanglement In One-dimensional Quantum Scattering
authors: V\'ictor M. Villalba
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study resonance-controlled post-selected mode entanglement in a one-dimensional quantum-scattering model. Two incoming electrons scatter independently from a symmetric double-barrier structure and the sector with one reflected and one transmitted electron is selected. The idealised delta-function barriers used in earlier work are replaced by exponentially localised cusp barriers, [MATH], for which the single-barrier scattering problem is exactly solvable in terms of modified Bessel functions of imaginary order. We derive the corresponding reflection and transmission amplitudes, verify their current normalisation and validate them independently by direct numerical integration. Two separated cusp barriers are then combined through a Fabry-P\'erot composition, whose accuracy is quantified by solving the full two-centre Schr\"odinger equation. In the well-separated regime the approximation reproduces the full resonance positions to high accuracy. The concurrence zeros are controlled by the resonance phase condition [MATH], with a continuously unwrapped single-barrier reflection phase [MATH]. We also calculate the post-selection probability [MATH], showing explicitly that large conditional concurrence can occur in a low-probability sector. Systematic scans in barrier width, integrated strength and reference momentum show that finite width can shift off-resonant concurrence maxima and, depending on the reference momentum, reduce their attainable height. The results identify resonance-controlled conditional entanglement as a robust feature of the well-separated double-barrier geometry rather than an artefact of the zero-range idealisation.
tldr: The paper analyzes resonance-controlled post-selected mode entanglement generated when two electrons scatter independently from a symmetric double-barrier structure and the one-reflected/one-transmitted sector is selected.
motivation: It aims to determine whether resonance-controlled conditional entanglement in one-dimensional scattering is a robust feature of realistic finite-width barriers rather than an artifact of idealized zero-range delta barriers.
method: The authors replace delta barriers with exactly solvable exponentially localized cusp barriers, derive reflection and transmission amplitudes, compose two barriers via a Fabry-Perot approximation validated against the full two-center Schrodinger equation, and compute concurrence zeros and post-selection probabilities.
result: They show that concurrence zeros are controlled by a resonance phase condition and that large conditional concurrence can occur in a low-probability post-selected sector, while finite barrier width can shift and reduce off-resonant concurrence maxima depending on reference momentum.
conclusion: Resonance-controlled conditional mode entanglement is robust in the well-separated double-barrier geometry, supporting it as a genuine scattering-induced entanglement effect rather than an idealization artifact.

title: Pulse-tube-vibration Induced Larmor Frequency Jitter In Anisotropic Kramers Spins
authors: R. Shaik, P. Kesarwani, S. Rajendran, S. E. Kubatkin, A. V. Danilov, S. E. de Graaf, V. Ranjan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the role of pulse-tube mechanical vibrations towards spin frequency noise in a cryogen-free dilution refrigerator. Our system comprises of a low mode-volume superconducting resonator coupled to 50 ppm [MATH] spins with highly anisotropic g-factors. By measuring single-shot spin echoes using narrow-bandwidth three-pulse sequences, we directly observe a vibration induced stochastic signal resulting from the spin's Larmor frequency moving into and out of the detection bandwidth. The sensitivity to these vibrations is substantially suppressed when a) the external magnetic field is aligned along the symmetry c-axis and b) spin temperature is modestly increased to 60~mK. We also benchmark the system as a quantum sensor for angular fluctuations, extracting a noise floor of 350 nanodegrees.

method: The authors couple a low-mode-volume superconducting resonator to 50 ppm anisotropic Kramers spins and use narrow-bandwidth three-pulse spin-echo sequences to detect vibration-induced stochastic frequency shifts.
result: Vibration sensitivity is strongly suppressed when the magnetic field is aligned with the symmetry c-axis and when the spin temperature is raised to 60 mK; the system is also benchmarked as an angular-fluctuation sensor with a 350 nanodegree noise floor.
conclusion: The work identifies vibration-induced Larmor frequency noise as a relevant decoherence channel for anisotropic spin ensembles in cryogen-free hybrid quantum systems and suggests mitigation via field orientation and temperature.

title: Symplectic Matroids, Stabilizer Codes, And Quantum Secret-Sharing

title: Reset Quantum Channels
authors: Alain Joye Thomas Argoud
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Reset Quantum Channels (RQCs), a class of quantum channels acting on a Hilbert space structured as a direct sum of an arbitrary number of subspaces. Within each subspace, the state evolves unitarily; across subspaces, it is transferred by measure-and-prepare resets along given states. In this general setting, we show that the determination of their invariant states reduces to a stochastic eigenvalue problem, whose size is set by the number of reset states rather than by the dimension of the Hilbert space, and we discuss the uniqueness of these states. We further address the primitivity and the spectrum of these channels, which we compute explicitly when the reset states commute with the unitary evolutions. Applications include a small system coupled to several thermal reservoirs. We also consider random unitary evolutions and analyze the averages of the invariant states in this setup. Finally, we show that a suitable continuous-time limit yields Lindblad generators of reset type on the algebra of block-diagonal operators.
tldr: The paper introduces reset quantum channels on direct-sum Hilbert spaces and analyzes their invariant states, spectrum, primitivity, and continuous-time Lindblad limits.
motivation: It aims to model quantum evolution that combines unitary dynamics inside subspaces with measure-and-prepare resets between subspaces, motivated by open quantum systems coupled to reservoirs.
method: The authors reduce the invariant-state problem to a stochastic eigenvalue problem whose size depends on the number of reset states, and study uniqueness, primitivity, spectrum, random unitary averages, and a continuous-time limit.
result: They show that invariant states can be found via a reduced stochastic eigenproblem, compute the spectrum explicitly when reset states commute with the unitaries, and derive reset-type Lindblad generators in the continuous-time limit.
conclusion: Reset quantum channels provide a tractable framework for reset dynamics, with applications including small systems coupled to multiple thermal reservoirs.

title: Physical Learning For Autonomous Tuning Of Spin Qubits In Electrostatically Defined Quantum Dots
authors: Leonardo Gaytan, Bradley Lloyd, Paul Kliewer, Chandler Wilburn, Lincoln D. Carr, Adam Mccaughan, Sonia Buckley, Meenakshi Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tuning electrostatically defined quantum dots remains a primary bottleneck in the scalability of semiconductor spin qubits. While existing solutions rely on machine learning algorithms, these approaches require global information, introduce latency bottlenecks, and tax the limited cooling power available at cryogenic stages. Here, we demonstrate an FPGA-in-the-loop learning paradigm that bypasses digital computing overhead by utilizing multiplexed gradient descent (MGD) for tuning. Implemented on an FPGA and an emulated quantum dot device, our system autonomously tracks environmental drift, dynamically recovers from discrete charge jumps, and maintains steady-state stabilization in low signal-to-noise ratio regimes, without prior knowledge of the device's cross-capacitance matrix. The system also navigates the charge-stability landscape to stabilize the quantum dot around optimal operating points. These results demonstrate a ``compute-in-place'' platform, with a logic and power footprint suited to future cryo-CMOS integration, that provides autonomous stabilization of quantum dots at desired operating points, creating an auto-tuning system for spin qubits that is resilient to electrostatic drifts, changing noise profiles, and two-level fluctuations.
tldr: The paper demonstrates an FPGA-in-the-loop physical learning system using multiplexed gradient descent to autonomously tune and stabilize electrostatically defined quantum dots for spin qubits.
motivation: Tuning quantum dots is a major scalability bottleneck for semiconductor spin qubits, and existing machine-learning approaches require global information, introduce latency, and consume scarce cryogenic cooling power.
method: The authors implement multiplexed gradient descent on an FPGA coupled to an emulated quantum dot device, enabling autonomous tuning without prior knowledge of the device cross-capacitance matrix.
result: The system tracks environmental drift, recovers from discrete charge jumps, maintains stabilization at low signal-to-noise ratios, and navigates the charge-stability landscape to optimal operating points.
conclusion: This compute-in-place approach provides a low-latency, low-power auto-tuning platform suitable for future cryo-CMOS integration and resilient stabilization of spin-qubit quantum dots.

title: Nanoscale Single-electron Box With A Floating Lead For Quantum Sensing: Modelling And Device Characterization
authors: Nikolaos Petropoulos, Xutong Wu, Andrii Sokolov, Panagiotis Giounanlis, Imran Bashir, Mike Asker, Dirk Leipold, Andrew K. Mitchell, Robert B. Staszewski, Elena Blokhina
abstract: ArXiv:2404.15002v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present an in-depth analysis of a single-electron box (SEB) biased through a floating node technique that is common in charge-coupled devices (CCDs). The device is analyzed and characterized in the context of single-electron charge-sensing techniques for integrated silicon quantum dots (QD). The unique aspect of our SEB design is the incorporation of a metallic floating node, strategically employed for sensing and precise injection of electrons into an electrostatically formed QD. To analyse the SEB, we propose an extended multi-orbital Anderson impurity model (MOAIM), adapted to our nanoscale SEB system, that is used to predict theoretically the behaviour of the SEB in the context of a charge-sensing application. The validation of the model and the sensing technique has been carried out on a QD fabricated in a fully depleted silicon on insulator (FDSOI) process on a 22-nm technological node. We demonstrate the MOAIM's efficacy in predicting the observed electronic behavior and elucidating the complex electron dynamics and correlations in the SEB. The results of our study reinforce the versatility and precision of the model in the realm of nanoelectronics and highlight the practical utility of the metallic floating node as a mechanism for charge injection and detection in integrated QDs. Finally, we identify the limitations of our model in capturing higher-order effects observed in our measurements and propose future outlooks to reconcile some of these discrepancies.
tldr: The paper models and characterizes a nanoscale single-electron box with a metallic floating node for charge sensing and controlled electron injection into integrated silicon quantum dots.
motivation: Precise charge sensing and electron injection are important for integrated silicon quantum-dot platforms, and the authors aim to validate a floating-node single-electron-box design for this purpose.
method: They adapt an extended multi-orbital Anderson impurity model to the nanoscale single-electron box and validate it against a quantum dot fabricated in a 22-nm fully depleted silicon-on-insulator process.
result: The model predicts the observed electronic behavior, clarifies complex electron dynamics and correlations, and demonstrates the practical utility of the floating node for charge detection and injection, while also identifying limitations in capturing higher-order effects.
conclusion: The study supports the versatility of the model for nanoelectronic device characterization and highlights the floating-node single-electron box as a useful mechanism for integrated quantum-dot charge sensing, with future work needed to resolve remaining discrepancies.

title: Cavity-Controlled Hysteresis And Multilevel Molecular Switching In Hybrid Optomechanics
authors: Hugo Molinares, Ra\'ul Coto, Vitalie Eremeev, Eduardo Chamorro
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate cavity-controlled hysteresis and multilevel molecular switching in a hybrid molecular optomechanical system composed of a plasmonic nanocavity, a Fabry-P\'erot cavity, and an ensemble of molecular vibrations. Molecular-plasmonic optomechanical interaction together with cavity-plasmon hybridization produce bistability and dynamical hysteresis, leading to a history-dependent optical and molecular response. An analytical treatment of the steady-state equations shows that the auxiliary cavity renormalizes the effective optical linewidth and detuning, while the collective molecular interaction generates an effective nonlinearity. Together, these effects enable control of the hysteretic regime through optical detuning, cavity-plasmon coupling, and molecular ensemble size. Beyond bistability, pulsed excitation generates staircase-like molecular dynamics, with ascending or descending vibrational populations depending on the optical driving configuration. In particular, the FP cavity controls the buildup of vibrational excitation, while simultaneous driving of both optical modes enables stepwise vibrational depletion. These results establish hybrid molecular optomechanical systems as a tunable platform for history-dependent and pulse-driven molecular dynamics, with potential applications in nanoscale memory, multilevel information processing, and optically controlled molecular switching.
tldr: The paper analyzes cavity-controlled bistability, hysteresis, and multilevel vibrational switching in a hybrid plasmonic-Fabry-Pérot molecular optomechanical system.
motivation: Hybrid molecular optomechanics may enable history-dependent optical memory and multilevel information processing, but the conditions for controlling hysteretic and stepwise molecular dynamics need characterization.
method: The authors use analytical steady-state equations and pulsed-excitation dynamics to study how cavity-plasmon hybridization, auxiliary-cavity renormalization, and collective molecular nonlinearity govern the system response.
result: Optical detuning, cavity-plasmon coupling, and molecular ensemble size tune the hysteretic regime, while pulsed driving produces staircase-like vibrational population buildup or depletion depending on the optical driving configuration.
conclusion: The system is a tunable platform for optically controlled molecular switching and nanoscale memory, although the work does not demonstrate qubit-coupled or clearly quantum-coherent operation.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Key Distribution Hardware Across Operating Conditions
authors: Jerry Horgan, Indrakshi Dey, Hajar Bennouri, Daniel C. Kilper
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is entering national fibre networks, but published secret key rates (SKRs) are measured over different distances, wavelengths, classical traffic loads and clock rates, so systems are hard to compare. We write the SKR as the product of the transmitter clock rate, the channel transmittance and the secret key per received pulse. This third factor, the noise-normalised key rate (NNKR), needs four commonly reported parameters and depends mainly on the equipment wherever the SKR is proportional to transmittance. A companion metric, the implementation efficiency (IE), compares the SKR with the ideal key rate of its channel, including classical-traffic noise. For fixed loss-limited equipment, NNKR is independent of channel loss, whereas the fraction of the repeaterless bound varies 1.6-fold over 2-25 dB. An analytic model relates the flat loss range of NNKR to the detector noise count rate and dead time. We apply both metrics to ten published coexistence experiments, and NNKR to 42,115 measurements from four systems of two vendors and four high-rate laboratory systems. For one production system, NNKR has a 6.9% coefficient of variation over 17 dB of attenuation and agrees within 0.7 dB with three of four published deployments of that platform. Under coexistence, that platform's NNKR and IE stay within 0.5 dB of their standalone values. In decibels, NNKR is a sum of component penalties, as in an optical link budget, and for one laboratory system the budget from its published parameters and measured secure fraction closes within 0.3 dB.
tldr: The paper proposes benchmarking metrics for comparing QKD hardware performance across distances, wavelengths, traffic loads, and clock rates.
motivation: Published QKD secret key rates are difficult to compare because they are measured under heterogeneous operating conditions and hardware assumptions.
method: The authors decompose the secret key rate into clock rate, channel transmittance, and a noise-normalised key rate (NNKR), introduce implementation efficiency (IE), and apply these metrics to published coexistence experiments and large measurement datasets.
result: NNKR is shown to be stable across loss for fixed loss-limited equipment, varies relative to the repeaterless bound, and can be expressed as a link-budget-like sum of component penalties; one production system shows a 6.9% coefficient of variation over 17 dB.
conclusion: NNKR and IE provide practical benchmarking tools for QKD hardware, but the work is primarily an applied hardware-performance characterization rather than a new QKD protocol or information-theoretic security result.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the lack of comparability among published secret key rates (SKRs) in quantum key distribution (QKD) systems, which are measured under disparate conditions (distance, wavelength, classical traffic, clock rate). The authors propose factoring the SKR into three components: the transmitter clock rate, the channel transmittance, and a noise-normalised key rate (NNKR) defined as the secret key per received pulse. They argue that NNKR, which depends mainly on equipment parameters and is independent of channel loss in the loss-limited regime, provides a fairer comparison metric. A companion metric, implementation efficiency (IE), compares the achieved SKR to the ideal key rate of the channel, including classical-traffic noise. An analytic model links the flat loss range of NNKR to detector noise count rate and dead time. The authors apply these metrics to ten published coexistence experiments and to 42,115 measurements from four commercial systems (two vendors) and four high-rate laboratory systems. For one production system, NNKR shows a 6.9% coefficient of variation over 17 dB of attenuation and agrees within 0.7 dB with three of four published deployments. Under coexistence, that platform's NNKR and IE remain within 0.5 dB of standalone values. In decibels, NNKR decomposes into a sum of component penalties, analogous to an optical link budget, and for one laboratory system the budget closes within 0.3 dB.
key_contributions: Proposes the noise-normalised key rate (NNKR) as a device-centric metric that factors out channel loss and clock rate, enabling fair comparison of QKD systems across different implementations.
Introduces implementation efficiency (IE) to benchmark SKR against the ideal key rate of the channel, incorporating classical-traffic noise.
Develops an analytic model relating the flat loss range of NNKR to detector noise count rate and dead time, providing a physical interpretation of the metric's loss independence.

Applies the metrics to a large dataset: ten coexistence experiments and 42,115 measurements from eight systems, demonstrating robustness and consistency (e.g., 6.9% coefficient of variation over 17 dB for one production system).
Shows that NNKR can be expressed as a sum of component penalties in decibels, analogous to an optical link budget, and validates this budget closure within 0.3 dB for a laboratory system.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is primarily analytical and empirical. The authors decompose the SKR into clock rate × transmittance × NNKR, arguing that NNKR isolates equipment performance from channel loss. They derive an analytic model for the loss range over which NNKR remains flat, linking it to detector dark count rate and dead time. The empirical validation uses a large corpus of published data: ten coexistence experiments and 42,115 measurements from commercial and laboratory systems. The analysis includes statistical measures such as coefficient of variation and decibel-based penalty decomposition. The approach is sound for comparing systems under the assumption that SKR is proportional to transmittance, which holds in the loss-limited regime. However, the reliance on published data may introduce inconsistencies in measurement conditions, and the analytic model assumes specific detector behavior that may not generalize to all QKD implementations.

It agrees within 0.7 dB with three of four published deployments of that platform, demonstrating reproducibility. title: Stinespring's Dilation, Universal-NOT, And Limitations Of Quantum Uncoupled Learning
authors: Pucheng Xiong Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncoupled learning, in which players know only their own payoff, are a standard model of decentralized learning toward Nash equilibrium. We study their quantum counterpart, where strategies are quantum states and, in each round, a player receives a physical copy of their opponent's current strategy and updates their own state by a quantum channel. This adds to uncoupledness a constraint with no classical analogue: every update must be physically realizable. In fact, this constraint is decisive in conjugation games, in which Bob has a strictly dominant pure strategy and Alice's unique best response is its transpose. In this work, we show some limitations of uncoupled (learning) dynamics in finding the Nash equilibrium for conjugation games. First, we prove that no autonomous, memoryless, uncoupled dynamics converge to Nash equilibrium in a family of four single-qubit conjugation games. Specifically, any memoryless channel that keeps all four equilibria fixed will leave Alice's strategy frozen. This result also extends to [MATH] games on [MATH]-qubit registers. Second, we show that this barrier disappears with a small classical memory: for any finite family of [MATH] pure targets, a guess-and-test rule with [MATH] classical bits converges to equilibrium, with an explicit bound on its convergence rate. Finally, we prove that no finite memory, classical or quantum, suffices for the continuum of all pure-qubit targets. Our proof of the impossibility for memoryless channels relies on Stinespring's dilation theorem, while the impossibility for finite-memory channels relies on the optimal universal-NOT (in)fidelity bound by Buek, Hillery, and Werner.
tldr: The paper proves fundamental limitations of quantum uncoupled learning dynamics for conjugation games, showing that physically realizable channel updates prevent memoryless convergence and that finite classical memory helps only for finite target sets.
motivation: Uncoupled learning is a standard decentralized model for reaching Nash equilibrium, and its quantum counterpart adds the constraint that every strategy update must be a physically realizable quantum channel.
method: The authors model quantum uncoupled dynamics in conjugation games and use Stinespring's dilation theorem to prove impossibility for memoryless channels, plus the optimal universal-NOT infidelity bound to rule out finite-memory convergence for a continuum of pure-qubit targets.
result: No autonomous memoryless uncoupled dynamics converge to Nash equilibrium in a family of four single-qubit conjugation games, while a guess-and-test rule with finite classical memory converges for any finite family of pure targets, but no finite memory suffices for all pure-qubit targets.
conclusion: Physical realizability imposes decisive barriers on quantum uncoupled learning; classical memory can overcome them only in finite-target settings, not universally.

title: Unconventional Photon Blockade In Second-Order Nonlinearity Coupled Cavities With Asymmetric Dissipation
authors: Zhi-Qiang Zhang, Xiao-Ai Zhang, Yan-Zhe Song, Meng-Li Guo, Yan-Hui Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the unconventional photon blockade in a second-order nonlinearity coupled double-cavity system with asymmetric dissipation. By treating the cavity decay rates as independent parameters, we analytically derive two exact families of optimal blockade conditions. While the first family recovers and generalizes the symmetric-dissipation results of previous studies, the second family, arising uniquely from an asymmetric dissipation ratio of [MATH], completely locks the relative phase of the interference pathways. Importantly, we find that this asymmetric dissipation not only renders the optimal blockade condition strictly immune to frequency detuning, but also enhances the blockade depth by an order of magnitude compared to the resonant case. Furthermore, the mean photon number remains almost unaffected, proving that this enhanced robustness is achieved without sacrificing the brightness of the single-photon source. These findings offer a promising route toward robust single-photon generation in passive cavities with second-order nonlinearity.
tldr: The paper analytically studies unconventional photon blockade in a second-order nonlinearity coupled double-cavity system with asymmetric dissipation to achieve robust single-photon generation.
motivation: Unconventional photon blockade offers a route to single-photon sources without strong nonlinearities, but robustness against detuning and dissipation asymmetry needs better understanding.
method: The authors treat the two cavity decay rates as independent parameters and derive exact analytical conditions for optimal photon blockade in a coupled nonlinear cavity system.
result: They identify two families of blockade conditions, one generalizing symmetric-dissipation results and another enabled by asymmetric dissipation that locks interference phases, removes detuning sensitivity, and enhances blockade depth by an order of magnitude without reducing brightness.
conclusion: Asymmetric dissipation provides a robust mechanism for single-photon generation in passive second-order nonlinear cavities, though the work is primarily a quantum-optics platform proposal rather than a direct quantum-information or hybrid-system study.

title: Augmenting Quantum Neural Networks With Contractive Layers
authors: Pengfei Zhang Bolin Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical neural networks combine diverse layers with complementary roles to achieve rich expressive capabilities across complex learning tasks. Rapid advances in quantum science and technology have motivated growing interest in their quantum counterparts, quantum neural networks, raising the question of how their expressivity can be enhanced through the design of new quantum layers. Of particular interest are layers that enrich the accessible function space while introducing only a small number of additional trainable parameters. In this Letter, we introduce the contractive layer as a promising building block for quantum neural networks. This layer comprises all-to-all couplings governed by a single trainable parameter, enabling efficient control of quantum information flow while maintaining experimental relevance to Rydberg atom arrays. Using observable learning as a benchmark, we show that contractive layers enhance expressivity more efficiently than simply increasing the depth of conventional brick-wall circuits. This advantage stems from a systematic increase in the accessible target-space dimension per trainable parameter. We further demonstrate similar improvements in image recognition tasks. These results highlight contractive layers as a practical route to expressive quantum neural networks on near-term quantum devices.
tldr: The paper introduces contractive layers for quantum neural networks, showing they improve expressivity with few trainable parameters and are compatible with Rydberg atom arrays.
motivation: Quantum neural networks need efficient ways to enhance expressivity without drastically increasing circuit depth or parameter count, especially on near-term hardware.
method: The authors define a contractive layer with all-to-all couplings controlled by a single trainable parameter, benchmark it on observable learning and image recognition, and compare it with deeper brick-wall circuits.
result: Contractive layers provide a more efficient increase in accessible target-space dimension per trainable parameter than simply increasing depth, yielding improved performance in the tested tasks.
conclusion: Contractive layers offer a practical building block for expressive quantum neural networks on near-term quantum devices such as Rydberg atom arrays.

title: Harnessing Dephasing For Quantum Reservoir Computing With A Minimum Complexity Architecture: Applications To Nonlinear Time-Series Prediction
authors: Yicheng Song, Zhipeng Yang, Heng Fan, Gouhei Tanaka
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) exploits quantum dynamics for temporal information processing. Quantum noise affects the reservoir dynamics and can either impair computational performance or serve as a computational resource. However, the role of pure dephasing in Hamiltonian encoding QRC remains unclear. In this work, we propose a minimum complexity QRC model that harnesses pure dephasing in an open uniform XX chain. We show that, under suitable input encoding, pure dephasing can ensure the echo state and fading memory properties even without amplitude damping. Furthermore, in the presence of amplitude damping, the proposed quantum reservoir has distinct stationary states for distinct inputs, and introducing pure dephasing alters these states, thereby affecting the reservoir dynamics. Information processing capacity analysis shows that joint control of the two decoherence mechanisms regulates memory and nonlinearity, providing access to diverse capacity profiles. The proposed QRC achieves promising performance on synthetic benchmarks, while its 6-qubit configuration outperforms all three multi-reservoir echo state network baselines on over half of the real-world prediction tasks. These findings highlight pure dephasing as a computational resource for QRC.
tldr: The paper proposes a minimal-complexity quantum reservoir computing model using pure dephasing in an open uniform XX chain for nonlinear time-series prediction.
motivation: Quantum reservoir computing can exploit quantum noise as a resource, but the role of pure dephasing in Hamiltonian-encoding reservoirs is not well understood.
method: The authors analyze an open XX-chain reservoir with controlled input encoding and joint pure dephasing and amplitude damping, using echo-state/fading-memory properties and information processing capacity to characterize performance.
result: Pure dephasing helps ensure echo-state and fading-memory properties without amplitude damping, and joint control of dephasing and damping yields diverse memory-nonlinearity capacity profiles; the 6-qubit reservoir performs well on benchmarks and some real-world prediction tasks.
conclusion: Pure dephasing is identified as a useful computational resource for quantum reservoir computing, though the work is primarily an applied machine-learning study rather than an information-theoretic or thermodynamic result.

title: 60-cm-long In-vacuum Zerodur Optical Cavity For Optical Lattice Atom Interferometry
authors: Philip Wondrak, Paola Luna, Kenneth Nakasone, Andrei Zhukov, Michael Grisham, Garrett D. Cole, Po-Han Chen, Cristian D. Panda
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27328v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical cavities are widely used in atomic physics experiments to control the spatial geometry and spectral properties of atom-light interactions. Recently, an optical lattice generated by the pristine mode of an optical cavity was utilized to hold and extend the quantum coherence of atomic spatial superpositions. Here, we describe an in-vacuum optical cavity designed to enhance the spatial and temporal coherence of optical lattice atom interferometers to one millimeter wavepacket separations and one minute measurement durations. The cavity uses a rigid Zerodur spacer to suppress the negative effects of thermal drift and mechanical-acoustic vibrations on the atomic motional state. The 60 cm-long cavity spacer provides ample optical access for the laser beams and imaging optics necessary for the preparation, quantum control, and read-out of the atomic state, as well as room for various source mass configurations for localized gravitational measurements. An integrated differential pumping structure enables compatibility with ultrahigh-vacuum operation and optical interferometry allows for in-situ vibration monitoring. The performance of the optical cavity is methodically characterized: we measure mirror vibration noise with amplitude below 5 nm/[MATH] in a wide frequency range of 2 Hz - 100 kHz and a slow 15 MHz thermal drift of the cavity resonance over 47 hours, which can be readily stabilized with an integrated piezo. The optical cavity supports both 852-nm light for Raman transitions and 1064-nm light for the optical lattice, with a free spectral range matched to an integer divisor of the cesium ground-state hyperfine splitting.
tldr: The authors design, build and characterize a 60-cm in-vacuum Zerodur optical cavity that supports both Raman (852 nm) and optical-lattice (1064 nm) light to extend coherence in optical-lattice atom interferometers.
motivation: Cavity-generated optical lattices can hold and extend quantum coherence of atomic spatial superpositions, but thermal drift and acoustic vibration noise degrade the atomic motional state, limiting wavepacket separation and interrogation time in atom interferometers.
method: A rigid Zerodur spacer cavity with integrated differential pumping for ultrahigh vacuum, piezo-based resonance stabilization, and in-situ optical interferometric vibration monitoring is constructed and methodically characterized for mirror vibration noise and thermal drift.
result: Mirror vibration noise below 5 nm/sqrt(Hz) over 2 Hz–100 kHz and a slow 15 MHz resonance drift over 47 hours (stabilizable by piezo) are measured, with both 852 nm and 1064 nm supported and a free spectral range matched to an integer divisor of the Cs hyperfine splitting.
conclusion: The cavity provides a platform targeting millimeter-scale wavepacket separations and one-minute measurement durations, with ample optical access for quantum control, readout and source-mass configurations for localized gravitational measurements.

title: $l^1$ Stability Of The Entropy Power Inequality In $\mathbb{R}^d$ Without Moment Assumptions
authors: Norman El Fartass, Lampros Gavalakis, Ioannis Kontoyiannis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish qualitative stability in [MATH] and Ruzsa distance for Shannon's entropy power inequality in [MATH], without any moment assumptions. The proof uses the optimal transport argument by Rioul (2017), majorization bounds of density rearrangements, and the stability of the sharp form of Young's inequality due to Christ (2019). Along the way we also extend recent one-dimensional results on de Bruijn's identity, the continuity of differential entropy, and the equality case of the entropy power inequality to random vectors of any dimension.
tldr: This paper proves qualitative stability of Shannon's entropy power inequality in R^d without moment assumptions using optimal transport, rearrangement majorization, and sharp Young inequality stability.
motivation: The entropy power inequality is a foundational inequality in classical information theory, and quantitative stability versions are important for understanding near-equality cases. Existing stability results often require moment assumptions, which this work aims to remove.
method: The authors use Rioul's optimal transport argument, majorization bounds for density rearrangements, and Christ's stability result for the sharp form of Young's inequality. They also extend several one-dimensional results on de Bruijn's identity, entropy continuity, and the equality case to arbitrary dimensions.
result: They establish qualitative l1 and Ruzsa-distance stability for the entropy power inequality in R^d without any moment assumptions. Along the way, they generalize recent one-dimensional results to random vectors of any dimension.
conclusion: The paper advances the mathematical foundations of classical information theory by providing stability guarantees for the entropy power inequality under minimal assumptions. It is not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Metadata-Private Voice Communication Over Tor Using Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation
authors: Samuel Zeinali Yazdi Noah Zeinali Yazdi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encrypted voice communication systems commonly protect call content but expose significant metadata, including the network identities of both parties, call timing, and traffic patterns. Simultaneously, advances in quantum computing threaten the asymmetric primitives underlying conventional key exchange, creating a harvest-now, decrypt-later risk for long-lived sensitive communications. Existing systems address at most one of these concerns: secure VoIP applications such as Signal and Wire rely on centralized infrastructure and classical cryptography, while anonymous communication tools built on the Tor network support only text messaging and lack post-quantum key encapsulation. This paper presents SAPEC (Secure Anonymous Peer Exchange Communicator), a peer-to-peer voice communication system that simultaneously addresses anonymity, decentralization, and quantum resistance. SAPEC routes all traffic exclusively through Tor hidden services, concealing the IP addresses of both parties, and augments the standard TLS handshake with a custom protocol layer that performs ML-KEM-1024 key establishment, a settle on AES-256 symmetrical keys and mutual Dilithium identity verification before any audio is transmitted. All audio is subsequently encrypted under AES-256. A removable Crypto Ignition Key prevents identity key material from being stored on the device. Empirical evaluation across 45 independently circuit-rebuilt test runs yielded a median one-way audio delay of 355 milliseconds and a median connection setup time of 7.61 seconds on same-region Tor circuits, demonstrating that interactive voice communication over onion routing is practically achievable.
tldr: SAPEC is a peer-to-peer voice communication system that combines Tor hidden services for anonymity with ML-KEM-1024 post-quantum key encapsulation and Dilithium identity verification to prevent harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks.
motivation: Encrypted VoIP systems expose metadata such as caller identities, timing and traffic patterns, while quantum computing threatens classical key exchange; existing tools address only one of the two problems, since Tor-based tools are text-only and secure VoIP apps are centralized and classically encrypted.
method: All traffic is routed exclusively through Tor hidden services to hide both parties' IP addresses, a custom protocol layer augments TLS with ML-KEM-1024 key establishment, AES-256 symmetric encryption, and mutual Dilithium authentication before audio transmission, with a removable Crypto Ignition Key for key material.
result: Across 45 independently circuit-rebuilt test runs, the system achieved a median one-way audio delay of 355 ms and a median connection setup time of 7.61 s on same-region Tor circuits.
conclusion: Interactive voice communication over onion routing with post-quantum key encapsulation is practically achievable, though latency and setup overhead remain substantial.

title: Improved Digitization Bounds For U(1) Lattice Gauge Theory Via Semiclassical Analysis
authors: Yu Tong Di Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating lattice gauge theories on a digital quantum computer or using tensor network methods requires a finite-dimensional approximation of the gauge field, a process often called digitization. Controlling the resulting error is essential for assessing the accuracy and resource requirements of these simulations. In this work, we derive a digitization error bound for low-lying eigenstates of the Kogut--Susskind Hamiltonian for pure U(1) gauge theory and translate it into a bound on time-evolution error. Compared with existing bounds, our result achieves exponentially improved dependence on the inverse lattice spacing [MATH] and evolution time [MATH], together with improved dependence on the inverse coupling [MATH]. The key idea is to identify a small parameter in the Kogut--Susskind Hamiltonian and apply tools from semiclassical analysis. Specifically, we adapt Agmon's method to establish exponential decay of the error with the truncation threshold. These results sharpen estimates of the local Hilbert space dimension and qubit resources needed to simulate gauge theories near the continuum limit, at weak coupling, and over long times.
tldr: The paper derives improved digitization error bounds for simulating pure U(1) lattice gauge theory on digital quantum computers using semiclassical analysis.
motivation: Finite-dimensional truncation of gauge fields is necessary for digital quantum simulation and tensor-network methods, and tighter error bounds are needed to estimate qubit and local Hilbert-space resources near the continuum limit.
method: The authors identify a small parameter in the Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian and adapt Agmon's semiclassical method to prove exponential decay of digitization error for low-lying eigenstates, then translate this into time-evolution error bounds.
result: The new bounds show exponentially improved dependence on the inverse lattice spacing and evolution time, along with improved dependence on the inverse coupling, compared with existing digitization bounds.
conclusion: These sharper estimates refine resource requirements for simulating lattice gauge theories near the continuum limit, at weak coupling, and over long times.

title: Feshbach Projection Formalism For Resonant Electrodynamics
authors: Nikolai A. Vlasov, Ekaterina E. Maslova, Andrey Novitsky, Mikhail V. Rybin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open resonant photonic systems are widely described by effective non-Hermitian formalisms, such as temporal coupled-mode theory, which capture radiative decay through complex eigenfrequencies. In conventional formulations, however, these effective models remain largely phenomenological, lacking a direct microscopic connection to the underlying Maxwell equations. To bridge this gap, we present an analytically tractable light-matter framework based on the Feshbach projection formalism applied to classical electrodynamics. Starting from a coupled system of mechanical oscillator and a one-dimensional electromagnetic field, we construct a strictly Hermitian first-order Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that rigorously eliminating the electromagnetic degrees of freedom via the outgoing Green's function automatically generates a non-Hermitian mechanical operator. Crucially, the resulting radiative damping is determined by the local electromagnetic response rather than introduced ad hoc. Furthermore, we extend this framework to two spatially separated dipoles and show how field retardation transforms a finite set of discrete modes into a countably infinite Fabry-Perot-like spectrum as the separation deviates from zero. The proposed framework provides an intuitive yet rigorous foundation for deriving effective non-Hermitian dynamics directly from conservative light-matter interactions.
tldr: The authors develop a Feshbach projection formalism for classical electrodynamics that derives effective non-Hermitian radiative damping rigorously from a Hermitian light-matter Hamiltonian, and extend it to retarded dipole-dipole coupling.
motivation: Effective non-Hermitian models such as temporal coupled-mode theory are widely used for open resonant photonic systems but remain phenomenological, lacking a microscopic derivation from Maxwell's equations.
method: Starting from a coupled mechanical oscillator and one-dimensional electromagnetic field, they construct a Hermitian first-order Hamiltonian and eliminate the field degrees of freedom via the outgoing Green's function, yielding an effective non-Hermitian mechanical operator; the approach is then applied to two spatially separated dipoles.
result: Radiative damping emerges from the local electromagnetic response rather than being inserted by hand, and field retardation converts a finite set of discrete modes into a countably infinite Fabry-Perot-like spectrum as dipole separation becomes nonzero.
conclusion: The framework provides an intuitive yet rigorous route from conservative light-matter interactions to effective non-Hermitian dynamics, offering a microscopic foundation for coupled-mode descriptions of open photonic resonators.

title: Trotter Error Bounds In Lean 4 With A Cancellation-Aware Analysis Of The Fourth-Order Suzuki Formula
authors: Bingyu Xia, Jue Xu, Yue Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formalize the commutator-scaling bound of Childs et al. in Lean 4. For skew-adjoint generators, the local order condition gives an explicit integer step count sufficient to meet a prescribed error tolerance. We apply the theorem in Lean to the binary fourth-order Suzuki formula. For this formula we can also account for cancellation within and between steps. Using local remainder estimates of Casas and Murua, we sum the signed quintic and centered seventh-degree error terms after conjugating each to the interaction picture. For every positive integer step count, we bound the difference between this sum and the global error operator. At fixed time the explicit remainder is eighth order in the step size, and the integral of the conjugated quintic term gives the exact leading error coefficient. The Lean proofs cover the two-generator finite-sum estimates, including the spectral norm for complex matrices. On five ten-site nearest-neighbor Heisenberg instances at time [MATH] and tolerance [MATH], the transported sum meets the tolerance at a mean of [MATH] steps. Taking a separate norm at each step with the same polynomial and remainder gives a mean first crossing between [MATH] and [MATH] steps. The accumulated Casas--Murua local bound at [MATH] gives a mean of [MATH] steps.
tldr: The paper formalizes commutator-scaling Trotter error bounds in Lean 4 and applies them to a cancellation-aware analysis of the fourth-order Suzuki formula.
motivation: The authors aim to provide machine-checked, rigorous error bounds for Trotterized quantum simulation and to exploit cancellation effects to obtain tighter step-count estimates.
method: They formalize the Childs et al. commutator-scaling bound in Lean 4, apply it to the binary fourth-order Suzuki formula, and use Casas--Murua local remainder estimates with interaction-picture conjugation to sum signed error terms.
result: The analysis yields an explicit eighth-order remainder in step size, the exact leading error coefficient from the conjugated quintic term, and benchmark step counts on ten-site Heisenberg instances.
conclusion: The work delivers formally verified Trotter error bounds and a cancellation-aware method that can reduce step counts for Hamiltonian simulation.

title: Structure-preserving Compression Of Matrix Product States
authors: Pouriya Ghadimi, Maximilian Fr\"ohlich, Aaron Sander, Martin Eigel, Richard M. Milbradt
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matrix product state time evolution relies on compression to control the growth of bond dimensions, but compression can break the conservation laws of the equation being solved. A truncation is not the flow of a Hermitian generator, so even a small truncation error can violate exact algebraic identities of the Schr\"odinger equation. For any matrix product state integrator that leaves the state in canonical form with an orthogonality center, a scalar correction restores an admissible global invariant after compression whenever the resulting scalar quadratic constraint equation admits a real root, without enlarging any bond dimension. Rank-preserving recovery searches other canonical centers when that correction fails. The geometry of the low-rank manifold provides sufficient conditions for conservation by the fixed-rank projected flow and bounds what corrections within a frozen center frame can achieve. Numerical experiments demonstrate that recovery can be required even along accurate truncated trajectories.
tldr: The paper proposes structure-preserving compression methods for matrix product state time evolution that restore global invariants after truncation without increasing bond dimension.
motivation: Matrix product state time evolution relies on compression to control bond-dimension growth, but truncation can break conservation laws and exact algebraic identities of the Schrödinger equation.
method: For canonical-form MPS integrators with an orthogonality center, a scalar correction restores an admissible global invariant when a scalar quadratic constraint has a real root; otherwise rank-preserving recovery searches other canonical centers. The low-rank manifold geometry gives sufficient conservation conditions and bounds correction capabilities within a frozen center frame.
result: Numerical experiments show that recovery can be required even along accurate truncated trajectories, demonstrating that small truncation errors can violate exact invariants.
conclusion: Structure-preserving compression can enforce global invariants in MPS time evolution without enlarging bond dimensions, subject to geometric and algebraic conditions on the correction.

title: Monolithic Ultraviolet-to- Near Infrared Photodetection Enabled By An Aluminium Oxide Photonic Platform
authors: Firehun T. Dullo, Marco Povoli, Ozhan Koybasi, Michael N. Getz, Daniel N. Wright
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Broadband photonic integrated circuits require waveguide platforms that combine low optical loss across a wide spectral range with integrated photodetection. Here we demonstrate a monolithically integrated atomic-layer-deposited (ALD) aluminium oxide (Al[MATH]O[MATH])-on-silicon platform enabling waveguide-coupled photodetection from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared. The architecture employs evanescent coupling between low-loss Al[MATH]O[MATH] waveguides and silicon p-i-n photodiodes. The platform supports photodetection at 375, 658 and 780 nm, extending integrated silicon photodetection into the ultraviolet. The devices exhibit linear photocurrent scaling with optical power, dark currents of approximately 2 pA at 50 V reverse bias and nanosecond-scale temporal response. We further demonstrate centimetre-scale ultraviolet Mach-Zehnder interferometer circuits with integrated photodiodes. The same detector architecture is implemented with Si[MATH]N[MATH] waveguides, whereas the lower ultraviolet propagation loss of Al[MATH]O[MATH] enables an approximately 15-fold higher photodetection response at 375 nm. These results establish ALD Al[MATH]O[MATH] as a broadband integrated photonics platform for sensing, spectroscopy and quantum technologies.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a monolithic Al2O3-on-silicon photonic platform with waveguide-coupled photodetection from ultraviolet to near-infrared wavelengths.
motivation: Broadband photonic integrated circuits need low-loss waveguides and integrated photodetection across a wide spectral range, including the ultraviolet.
method: The authors use atomic-layer-deposited Al2O3 waveguides evanescently coupled to silicon p-i-n photodiodes and compare performance with Si3N4 waveguides.
result: The platform achieves photodetection at 375, 658, and 780 nm with pA-level dark currents, nanosecond response, and about 15-fold higher UV response than Si3N4-based devices.
conclusion: ALD Al2O3 is established as a broadband integrated photonics platform for sensing, spectroscopy, and potential quantum technologies.

title: Quantum Computing For Gearing Down Complex Many-fermion Problems
authors: Weijie Du, Filippo Fornetti, James P. Vary
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing unlocks exciting opportunities to extend first-principles calculations of quantum many-body systems beyond classical computing limits. Despite advances in algorithms and proof-of-principle experiments, large-scale {\it ab initio} calculations on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices remain challenging. We introduce a quantum-classical framework that identifies compact single-particle bases to bring otherwise intractable many-fermion problems within classical reach while preserving an accurate ground-state description. We develop an efficient adaptive search scheme driven by simulated annealing that jointly optimizes natural-orbital-guided transformations and active-space selections. A quantum-assisted ground-state estimator provides search guidance using low-depth circuits and relaxed accuracy requirements, making the framework promising for NISQ devices. We demonstrate the framework's applicability for the nuclear structure of the oxygen isotopes. Our framework opens a new route to tackling complex {\it ab initio} many-fermion problems across disciplines through quantum-assisted basis reduction.
tldr: A quantum-classical framework uses simulated annealing and low-depth quantum-assisted ground-state estimation to find compact single-particle bases and active spaces that bring otherwise intractable many-fermion problems within classical reach.
motivation: Large-scale ab initio many-body calculations, such as nuclear structure, remain out of reach for NISQ devices, so the authors seek to use quantum resources only as guidance to reduce the classical computational burden.
method: An adaptive simulated-annealing search jointly optimizes natural-orbital-guided basis transformations and active-space selections, with a quantum-assisted ground-state estimator using shallow circuits providing relaxed-accuracy search guidance.
result: The framework is demonstrated on oxygen isotopes, showing that quantum-assisted basis reduction yields compact bases that preserve an accurate ground-state description.
conclusion: Quantum-assisted basis reduction offers a new route to tackling complex ab initio many-fermion problems across disciplines on near-term devices.

title: Large Deviations, Effective Dynamics, And Dynamical Phase Transitions In Random Maps
authors: \'angela Tajuelo-Valbuena, Jorge Hidalgo, Ricardo Guti\'errez, Carlos P\'erez-Espigares
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large deviation theory provides a natural framework to characterize rare fluctuations of time-averaged observables in deterministic and stochastic systems. Building on previous results for deterministic chaotic maps, here we extend the Doob transform to random maps, constructing an effective dynamics in which rare events become typical. This makes it possible to directly reproduce the dynamics of rare trajectories that are exponentially difficult to sample under the original dynamics. We further apply spectral large-deviation methods to characterize dynamical phase transitions in random maps. The spectral structure of the tilted operator provides insight into the mechanisms underlying these transitions and, in particular, allows us to identify the appropriate initial states that select one dynamical phase or another. Our results extend the connection between large deviation theory, spectral methods, and effective dynamics to random chaotic maps, providing a general framework to study rare events and dynamical phase transitions in these systems.
