tldr: The paper extends large-deviation and Doob-transform methods to random chaotic maps to study rare trajectories and dynamical phase transitions.
motivation: Large deviation theory characterizes rare fluctuations of time-averaged observables, but previous effective-dynamics constructions were developed mainly for deterministic chaotic maps.
method: The authors generalize the Doob transform to random maps, construct an effective dynamics for rare events, and use spectral large-deviation methods based on a tilted operator.
result: The approach reproduces exponentially rare trajectories under the original dynamics and identifies initial states that select different dynamical phases via the spectral structure of the tilted operator.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework connecting large deviations, spectral methods, and effective dynamics for rare events and dynamical phase transitions in random chaotic maps.

title: Fully Automated Discovery Of Phase Diagrams Using Agentic Large Language Models
authors: Robert Amelung, Maximilian N\"agele, Florian Marquardt
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classifying phases of matter and mapping out phase diagrams are central problems in physics. Recently, machine learning techniques have emerged as promising tools for phase classification, ranging from supervised learning to various unsupervised methods. However, these techniques provide limited qualitative insight into the discovered phases, typically work only for specific system classes, and do not by themselves efficiently map out the phase diagram. Autonomously constructing the phase diagram of a general system purely from measurements, without prior knowledge of the system, while also yielding qualitative understanding of the phases, remains an open task. In this work, we introduce Phasonaut, a two-agent framework that leverages the tool-use capabilities and broad knowledge of large language models (LLMs) to drive an active learning loop that constructs phase diagrams of physical systems and provides interpretations of the discovered phases. Starting from scratch, it iteratively selects and performs measurements, analyzes the resulting data, and segments the parameter domain into the phases it discovers. Phasonaut recovers the phase diagrams of classical and quantum spin systems to substantial precision. In the future, this framework could enable rapid exploration of systems with unknown phase diagrams, including in autonomously driven experiments.
tldr: Phasonaut, a two-agent LLM framework, autonomously discovers and interprets phase diagrams of classical and quantum spin systems through an active-learning measurement loop.
motivation: Existing machine-learning phase-classification methods offer little qualitative insight, are system-specific, and do not themselves map out phase diagrams; fully autonomous phase-diagram construction from measurements alone remains open.
method: Two LLM agents exploit tool-use and broad physics knowledge to iteratively select and perform measurements, analyze the resulting data, and segment the parameter space into discovered phases, starting with no prior system knowledge.
result: Phasonaut recovers phase diagrams of classical and quantum spin systems to substantial precision while providing qualitative interpretations of the phases found.
conclusion: Agentic LLM frameworks can automate exploratory phase-diagram mapping and may in future be deployed in autonomously driven experiments on systems with unknown phase diagrams.

title: Scheduling The Quantum Implementation Of The Trotter Decomposition For Hamiltonian Simulation
authors: Augustin Ho (graduate School Of Science And Technology, Keio University, \'ecole Des Mines de Saint-\'etienne), Naoki Yamamoto
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the quantum computational task for Hamiltonian simulation, the arrangement in which sub-Hamiltonians appear in the Trotter decomposition may have a large influence on the precision, under a given circuit complexity. In this paper, we design several scheduling strategies by combining two methods; that is, the existing simultaneous diagonalization scheme leveraged in order to guarantee the performance in a relatively short circuit depth, with a method inspired from a Trotter-Suzuki decomposition of the second or the fourth order for a better accuracy. By conducting numerical simulations on various Hamiltonian instances, we confirm a systematic advantage over previous methods. Thus, our proposal may eliminate the need of dealing with several Hamiltonian-dependent scheduling strategies.
tldr: The paper proposes scheduling strategies for arranging sub-Hamiltonians in Trotter decompositions to improve Hamiltonian simulation accuracy at fixed circuit depth.
motivation: The ordering of sub-Hamiltonians in Trotter-based Hamiltonian simulation can significantly affect precision for a given circuit complexity, motivating systematic scheduling strategies.
method: The authors combine simultaneous diagonalization, which performs well at short circuit depths, with second- and fourth-order Trotter-Suzuki-inspired scheduling schemes, and benchmark them numerically on various Hamiltonians.
result: Numerical simulations show a systematic accuracy advantage over previous scheduling methods across multiple Hamiltonian instances.
conclusion: The proposed combined scheduling approach may remove the need for Hamiltonian-dependent scheduling strategies in Trotter-based Hamiltonian simulation.

title: Consecutive Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanical Algorithms For Resolving The Spectra Of Legendre-type Differential Operators
authors: Tianchun Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quite comprehensive iterative algorithms based on consecutive supersymmetric quantum mechanics (SUSYQM) have been constructed heuristically, for resolving the eigenspectra of the Legendre operator and its associates parametrized in various coordinates, . On building these algorithms, the two symmetries supersymmetry and shape invariance symmetry hidden in these operators are brought to the fore as the only two governing principles, with the aids of the newly devised algebraic techniques such as the , as well as plain and . In view of their algebraic simplicity and elegance, high efficiency, as well as independence of traditional methods, some of these algorithms become the promising candidates to supplant the popular power series approach to the eigenspectra of Legendre-type operators.
tldr: The paper constructs iterative supersymmetric quantum mechanics (SUSYQM) algorithms for computing the eigenspectra of the Legendre operator and its relatives.
motivation: Traditional power-series methods for Legendre-type eigenvalue problems are cumbersome, so the author seeks algebraic approaches exploiting hidden supersymmetry and shape invariance.
method: Consecutive SUSYQM is combined with algebraic techniques (shape invariance, ladder-type factorizations) to build heuristic iterative algorithms in various coordinate parametrizations.
result: The algorithms reproduce eigenspectra efficiently and with algebraic simplicity, claimed to rival or surpass the power-series approach.
conclusion: SUSYQM-based iterative schemes are presented as promising replacements for conventional spectral methods for Legendre-type operators, though the work is purely mathematical-physics methodology.

title: Stable Phase Retrieval From Operator Measurements
authors: Deanna Needell, Yaniv Plan, Tomasz Szczepanski, \"ozg\"ur Y{\i}lmaz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A known result of Cahill, Casazza and Daubechies [Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. Ser. B3(2016), 63-76] states that no frame in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space does stable phase retrieval. We show that stable recovery becomes possible for more general operator measurements, but only at a single exponent. Given a system of bounded operators [MATH] on a real or complex Hilbert space [MATH], we study recovery of [MATH] up to a global phase from the quadratic measurements [MATH] and from their phase preserving square roots. We consider [MATH]-Bessel systems ([MATH]) for which we measure the quadratic data in [MATH] and the square root data in [MATH]. In infinite dimensions, we show that whenever [MATH], no [MATH]-Bessel system of operators does stable phase retrieval. In the case of [MATH], we show that stability still fails on any system of semidefinite operators. Nevertheless, we construct a system of rank-one operators, not all self-adjoint, for which stable recovery is possible. We also show that stability can be achieved on a system of self-adjoint operators of rank-two. For both types of measurements, we show that the stability can be tested on orthogonal pairs. This reduction preserves the optimal constant for quadratic measurements and, when the operators are semidefinite, for their phase preserving square roots. We deduce that in finite dimensions, uniqueness of recovery implies its stability. Finally, we show that whenever only the moduli of the measurements are retained, both the orthogonal reduction and the implication from uniqueness to stability can fail, already in dimension two. We also give second moment measurements in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) as a motivation for the quadratic model.
tldr: The paper studies stable phase retrieval from quadratic operator measurements in Hilbert spaces, showing stability is possible only at a special exponent and constructing operator systems that achieve it.
motivation: Phase retrieval traditionally uses frame measurements, but Cahill–Casazza–Daubechies showed no frame in infinite dimensions does stable phase retrieval. The authors ask whether more general operator measurements can overcome this limitation.
method: They analyze Bessel systems of bounded operators, comparing recovery from quadratic data and phase-preserving square-root data. They prove impossibility results for certain exponents and semidefinite operators, construct rank-one and rank-two self-adjoint systems with stability, and reduce stability testing to orthogonal pairs.
result: Stability fails for Bessel systems below a critical exponent and for semidefinite operators at the critical exponent. However, stable recovery is achievable using non-self-adjoint rank-one operators or self-adjoint rank-two operators. In finite dimensions, uniqueness implies stability for the quadratic model.
conclusion: General operator measurements can enable stable phase retrieval in infinite dimensions, unlike frames, but only under restricted exponent and operator-rank conditions. The results also clarify when orthogonal-pair reductions and uniqueness-to-stability implications fail for modulus-only measurements.

title: Post-Quantum Migration In Brownfield 5g Core Networks: Verified Hybrid Key Establishment, Performance, And Rollback
authors: Shubham Verma
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Migrating brownfield 5G Core networks to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is difficult because deployed network functions, base images, and TLS libraries evolve under different upgrade constraints. This paper evaluates a deployment-controlled migration strategy that enables hybrid post-quantum/traditional key establishment through externally deployed Boundary Cryptographic Execution Entities (BCEEs), without modifying participating network function source code. The approach is evaluated using the Open5GS AMF-NRF Service-Based Interface as a representative 5G Core scenario. Classical and hybrid configurations are compared under an unchanged mediation topology. Packet-level analysis confirms successful negotiation of X25519MLKEM768, and functional validation demonstrates that representative SBI procedures remain operational through the mediated path. In 120 NF-registration transactions, the median AMF-facing registration latency increased from 22.968 ms under the classical state to 26.351 ms under the hybrid state, reflecting a 3.383 ms (14.73 percent) increase, with a whole-block 95 percent confidence interval of [1.193, 7.872] ms. At the mediated TLS boundary, the hybrid configuration shows a 4.599 ms higher median segment-local TLS-establishment time than the classical configuration. These two reported differences reflect system-level runtime effects and do not isolate key-encapsulation cost. Packet evidence verifies rollback from hybrid-mediated operation to classical mediated operation and, separately, restoration of the native direct path. NF-facing compatibility legs remained plaintext and outside the hybrid post-quantum scope. The results demonstrate a packet-verifiable and manually reversible brownfield mechanism for introducing hybrid post-quantum key establishment on a controlled 5G SBI segment.
tldr: This paper evaluates a deployment-controlled migration strategy for hybrid post-quantum/traditional key establishment in brownfield 5G core networks using externally deployed boundary cryptographic entities.
motivation: Deployed 5G core networks face heterogeneous upgrade constraints, making migration to post-quantum cryptography difficult without modifying network function source code.
method: The authors use Open5GS AMF-NRF service-based interface as a representative scenario, compare classical and hybrid X25519MLKEM768 configurations under an unchanged mediation topology, and perform packet-level and latency measurements including rollback validation.
result: Hybrid operation showed a median AMF-facing registration latency increase of 3.383 ms (14.73%) and a 4.599 ms higher median TLS-establishment time; rollback to classical mediated operation and restoration of the native direct path were packet-verified.
conclusion: The results demonstrate a packet-verifiable and manually reversible brownfield mechanism for introducing hybrid post-quantum key establishment on a controlled 5G SBI segment, though compatibility legs remained plaintext and outside the post-quantum scope.

title: Parity-violating Optical Rotation In The Th-229 Nuclear Clock Transition
authors: Sebastian Lahs, Thorsten Schumm, Victor V. Flambaum, David Demille
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The exceptionally low-energy nuclear transition in [MATH]Th provides a new opportunity to study hadronic parity violation (PV) by optical methods. The PV nucleon--nucleus interaction admixes opposite-parity nuclear states into the [MATH] ground state and the [MATH] isomer, thereby inducing an electric-dipole amplitude [MATH] that interferes with the magnetic-dipole clock transition amplitude [MATH]. In a single-valence-neutron Nilsson model, we find [MATH]. This interference can be detected as a parity-violating nuclear optical rotation (PVNOR) of resonant laser light transmitted through a [MATH]Th-doped crystal. For a highly-doped CaF[MATH] crystal fiber, the estimated rotation is of order [MATH]. A crossed-polarizer measurement can reach this sensitivity with existing ultraviolet laser technology. We also analyze systematic effects in the form of optical birefringence, stray magnetic-field-induced Faraday rotation, and local crystal defects. Such a measurement would provide the first direct probe of the PV neutron-nucleus interaction constant, [MATH].
tldr: The paper proposes detecting hadronic parity violation via parity-violating optical rotation of laser light at the Th-229 nuclear clock transition in a doped crystal.
motivation: The exceptionally low-energy Th-229 nuclear transition offers a new optical route to probe parity-violating nucleon-nucleus interactions that are otherwise difficult to access.
method: Using a single-valence-neutron Nilsson model, the authors estimate the electric-dipole amplitude admixed into the nuclear clock transition and analyze its interference with the magnetic-dipole amplitude in a Th-229-doped CaF2 crystal fiber.
result: They predict a parity-violating optical rotation of order 10^-8 rad for a highly doped crystal fiber, detectable with existing ultraviolet laser technology via a crossed-polarizer measurement.
conclusion: Such an experiment could provide the first direct probe of the parity-violating neutron-nucleus interaction constant, but the work is primarily nuclear/atomic physics and precision metrology rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Benchmark Ne-like Transitions Of W, Re, Os, Ir, And Bi Measured By High-resolution Tes X-ray Spectroscopy With Absolute Energy Calibration
authors: G. Mondeel (clemson University, Massachusetts Institute Of Technology), C. A. Faiyaz (clemson University), Dipti (clemson University, National Institute Of Standards And Technology Gaithersburg), H. Staiger (clemson University, National Institute Of Standards And Technology Gaithersburg), L. Brent (loyola University Maryland, National Institute Of Standards And Technology Gaithersburg), A. C. Gall (auburn University, Center For Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian), C. I. Szabo (national Institute Of Standards And Technology Gaithersburg), G. O'neil (national Institute Of Standards And Technology Boulder), D. S. Swetz (national Institute Of Standards And Technology Boulder), P. Szypryt (national Institute Of Standards And Technology Boulder, University Of Colorado Boulder), J. W. Dean (national Institute Of Standards And Technology Boulder, University Of Colorado Boulder), Yu. Ralchenko (NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, University Of Maryland College Park), E. Takacs
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present high-resolution measurements of [MATH]-3 transitions in Ne-like tungsten, rhenium, osmium, iridium, and bismuth using a transition-edge sensor (TES) microcalorimeter. These measurements provide new benchmarks for Ne-like ions in the high-[MATH] regime ([MATH]), extending previous EBIT studies of the sequence. To achieve sub-eV accuracy, we developed a dedicated x-ray fluorescence source employing well-characterized K-shell emission lines from metallic elements. Our results offer stringent tests for relativistic atomic structure theories and demonstrate the advantage of TES spectroscopy for precision measurements in highly charged ions.
tldr: High-resolution TES microcalorimeter measurements of Ne-like W, Re, Os, Ir, and Bi M-shell transitions provide new benchmarks for relativistic atomic structure theory in highly charged ions.
motivation: Precision wavelengths for highly charged Ne-like ions in the high-Z regime are needed to test relativistic atomic structure calculations and to support astrophysical and plasma diagnostics, but existing EBIT data lack sub-eV accuracy.
method: A transition-edge sensor microcalorimeter was used to record x-ray emission from Ne-like ions, with absolute energy calibration provided by a dedicated x-ray fluorescence source using well-characterized K-shell emission lines of metallic elements.
result: Sub-eV-accuracy transition energies were obtained for five Ne-like ions, extending prior EBIT benchmark studies and enabling stringent tests of relativistic atomic theory.
conclusion: TES spectroscopy is shown to be a powerful tool for precision x-ray metrology of highly charged ions, though the work is atomic-physics metrology with no direct bearing on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Probabilistic Image Generation Conditioned On An Optical Latent Code
authors: Yu Shao, Haiqi Gao, Fuyan Wu, Ziyan Zhang, Junren Wen, Yuchuan Shao, Weidong Shen, Chenying Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While diffractive optical networks compress images into compact representations, such measurements have predominantly served discriminative inference or deterministic reconstruction. Here we demonstrate probabilistic image generation conditioned solely on a 16_bit binary optical latent code (OLC) formed by a diffractive encoder and binarized camera readout. The intentionally many-to-one mapping makes each OLC specify a class of OLC-compatible images rather than a unique reconstruction target. An OLC_conditioned conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) learns this distribution, while optical re-encoding promotes consistency between generated images and the measured OLC. Numerical characterization and proof-of-concept acquisition with a spatial light modulator_camera system establish the OLC as a physically accessible generative condition. On MNIST, samples generated from a single OLC vary in morphology while preserving class identity, and their optical-recognition accuracy reaches 81.6%, close to the 81.9% obtained from the source OLCs. These results link compact optical sensing to probabilistic synthesis of optically recognizable images.
tldr: The paper demonstrates probabilistic image generation conditioned on a compact 16-bit binary optical latent code produced by a diffractive encoder and camera readout.
motivation: Diffractive optical networks have mainly been used for discriminative inference or deterministic reconstruction, leaving probabilistic synthesis from physically accessible optical measurements underexplored.
method: A conditional variational autoencoder is trained to model the many-to-one distribution of images compatible with each optical latent code, with optical re-encoding used to enforce consistency between generated images and measured codes.
result: On MNIST, samples generated from a single optical latent code vary in morphology while preserving class identity, achieving 81.6% optical-recognition accuracy compared with 81.9% for source codes.
conclusion: The work links compact optical sensing to probabilistic image synthesis and establishes the optical latent code as a physically accessible generative condition.

title: How Many States Does An Exact Relaxation Model Need? Sharp State Complexity And Geometric Obstructions For Reversible Chains
authors: Murad Aznagulov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How many states does a reversible Markov model need to reproduce two prescribed relaxation modes exactly? We maximize the smaller of the two stationary coordinate variances over all finite reversible chains whose states lie in a given convex region and whose coordinates relax at rates [MATH] and [MATH]. Detailed balance turns this into the equilibrium of a tension-only cable network whose loads depend on the stationary masses. For the moment curve of the Wright-Fisher diffusion no finite chain is optimal: maximizing sequences converge to a unique beta law, and the best deficit with [MATH] states is of order [MATH]. We find the exact leading constant for states on the curve and for states in its convex hull, together with the optimal cube-root density of states. The hull constant is the curve constant times [MATH], [MATH]; at [MATH] the hull needs [MATH] times fewer states, although the limiting law is the same. For [MATH] any upward enlargement of the hull lowers the constant again. All lower bounds hold for arbitrary transition graphs. At every fixed number of states an optimizer exists. On a seven-gon the smallest optimal chain jumps from three to four states while the optimal value stays constant, and a family of polygons forces the state count to grow linearly with the number of sides. Monotone vector fields give exact upper certificates, which solve an asymmetric quadrilateral at all rates and 381 polygon-rate instances in exact arithmetic. We formulate a finite-realizability problem and a finite-dictionary conjecture for polygons, and derive state budgets and exclusion tests for finite kinetic models.
tldr: The paper studies the minimal number of states needed for finite reversible Markov chains to exactly reproduce prescribed relaxation modes, with sharp asymptotics and geometric obstructions.
motivation: It asks how many states an exact reversible relaxation model requires when matching two stationary coordinate variances and fixed relaxation rates.
method: The problem is reformulated via detailed balance as a tension-only cable network equilibrium, and asymptotic constants are derived for chains supported on the Wright-Fisher moment curve and its convex hull using lower bounds and monotone vector-field certificates.
result: No finite chain is optimal for the moment curve; optimal sequences converge to a beta law with explicit state-count deficits, and hull constants differ by a factor depending on parameters, with exact certificates for polygon-rate instances.
conclusion: The work provides sharp state-complexity bounds and exclusion tests for finite kinetic models, but it is a classical stochastic-process/mathematical modeling paper rather than a quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-systems contribution.

title: Verification Of Statistical Properties: Redefining The Possible
authors: Cl\'ement Canonne, Sam Polgar, Aditya Vikram Singh, Aravind Thyagarajan, Qiping Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the setting of Interactive Proof Systems for Distribution Testing, introduced by Chiesa and Gur (2018), showing that a simple twist on the task requirements may lead to dramatic improvements, allowing verifiers with constant sample complexity. We define and investigate the multi-prover and zero-knowledge versions of these interactive proof systems, using as flagship example the task of farness verification - the "dual" version of closeness testing. We hope our results will inspire others to investigate and analyze the power and limitations of multiple provers for distribution verification.
tldr: The paper revisits interactive proof systems for distribution testing and shows that modified task requirements enable constant-sample-complexity verifiers, including multi-prover and zero-knowledge variants.
motivation: Distribution testing and interactive proofs are central in classical theoretical computer science, and the authors seek to understand whether simple changes to verification tasks can yield dramatic efficiency gains.
method: The authors define and analyze interactive proof systems for distribution verification, focusing on farness verification as a dual to closeness testing, and extend the framework to multi-prover and zero-knowledge settings.
result: They demonstrate that verifiers can achieve constant sample complexity under the revised task requirements, and they establish properties of multi-prover and zero-knowledge versions of these systems.
conclusion: The work highlights the power and limitations of multiple provers for distribution verification and aims to inspire further study of interactive proofs in distribution testing.

title: Efficient Tensor Decomposition Of The Coulomb And Coulomb-like Potentials And Its Application To Probing Molecular Geometries Using A Quantum Computer
authors: James Brown, Masashi Takahashi, Robert Wodraszka, James Whitfield
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an efficient canonical polyadic decomposition of the Coulomb and Coulomb-like potentials in real-space grid representations suited to quantum computing applications. By decomposing the matrix elements of Coulomb-like potentials into low-rank Cartesian components, we achieve [MATH] T-gate scaling per Coulomb term, where [MATH] is the number of grid points (basis functions) per electron, while maintaining high accuracy. This opens a path to significantly reducing the number of basis functions (i.e., qubits) required compared to previous methods by utilizing improved representations of the Coulomb potential that converge faster with grid spacing. The decomposition is also valid for certain pseudopotentials, which can decrease the cost significantly compared to previous work. This efficient decomposition enables the application of block-encoding techniques at larger grid spacings than with previous decompositions, and can therefore be used for algorithms that do not require high energy accuracy. We apply this decomposed Coulomb potential to hydrogen atom energy levels, the helium ground-state energy, and the Hartree-Fock potential energy curve of LiH, and show that modest basis sizes achieve semi-quantitative to quantitative accuracy. As an example of where these faster-converging Coulomb representations can be used on a quantum computer, we discuss their application to probing low-energy molecular geometries, and we estimate the resulting reduction in the cost of real-time evolution.
tldr: The paper presents a low-rank tensor decomposition of Coulomb and Coulomb-like potentials for efficient quantum-computer simulation of molecular systems.
motivation: Efficiently representing Coulomb interactions is a bottleneck for quantum chemistry algorithms on quantum computers, especially when reducing qubit and gate costs.
method: The authors develop a canonical polyadic decomposition of Coulomb potentials into low-rank Cartesian components and apply block-encoding techniques to hydrogen, helium, and LiH examples.
result: The decomposition achieves improved T-gate scaling per Coulomb term and enables modest basis sizes to reach semi-quantitative to quantitative accuracy for energies and potential curves.
conclusion: The approach can reduce resource costs for real-time evolution and low-energy molecular geometry probing, but it is primarily a quantum-chemistry simulation contribution rather than a quantum-information-theory result.

title: Geometric Properties Of Wilsonian Flows Of Periodic Potentials In Two Dimensions
authors: Nathan O. Silvano Daniel G. Barci
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodic interactions can possess multiple competing minima and barriers, whose evolution under coarse-graining offers a geometric perspective complementary to the scaling of Fourier harmonics. We study this evolution in two dimensions by deriving a functional Wilsonian renormalization-group flow for a general smooth periodic potential and its running sine-Gordon frequency within a constant-kinetic projection. Reaction--diffusion and Burgers representations reveal two key properties of the flow: discrete translation symmetries are preserved, and the number of extrema can only remain constant or decrease. Consequently, the nonlinear generation of Fourier harmonics may accompany a progressive simplification of the potential landscape. We illustrate the role of symmetry with two complementary examples. A weak breaking of the [MATH]-translation symmetry allows a reduction from four extrema to two, whereas a non-sinusoidal interaction retaining this symmetry evolves from eight extrema to the four protected by its periodicity. These results highlight how symmetry and coarse-graining jointly reorganize competing minima and barriers in periodic interactions.
tldr: The paper derives a functional Wilsonian renormalization-group flow for smooth periodic potentials in two dimensions and analyzes how coarse-graining reorganizes minima and barriers.
motivation: Periodic interactions can have many competing extrema, and the authors seek a geometric complement to Fourier-harmonic scaling by tracking the potential landscape under coarse-graining.
method: They formulate a functional Wilsonian RG flow for a general smooth periodic potential and its running sine-Gordon frequency under a constant-kinetic projection, using reaction-diffusion and Burgers representations.
result: The flow preserves discrete translation symmetries and can only keep or reduce the number of extrema; examples show reductions from four to two extrema under weak symmetry breaking and from eight to four protected extrema for a non-sinusoidal interaction.
conclusion: Symmetry and coarse-graining jointly control the simplification of periodic potential landscapes, even when nonlinear Fourier harmonics are generated.

title: Coherence Lengths Of Laser Pointers
authors: Vaishnavi Rao Namakkal Ranga Rao, Marissa R. Godoy, Mark D. Sotnikov, Justin L. Oliver, Ayane Gomi, Bo Eickelberg, Mariana Rojas-Montoya, Henry B. Wahhab, Christopher L. Smallwood
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on the coherence lengths of low-cost green laser pointers in the midst of multimodal behavior using an optical interferometer based on noncollinear beam geometries and a CMOS detector array. Examined devices include three diode lasers and a frequency-doubled neodymium-emission diode-pumped solid state (DPSS) laser. Coherence length measurements are variable among devices, but values can nevertheless regularly exceed 10 cm. The work serves as a template for an advanced undergraduate physics laboratory experiment and may inspire new kinds of laser pointer devices utilizing interference effects as operative principles.
tldr: The paper measures coherence lengths of low-cost green laser pointers using a noncollinear optical interferometer and CMOS detector array.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize coherence properties of common laser pointers and provide a template for an advanced undergraduate physics laboratory experiment.
method: They use an optical interferometer with noncollinear beam geometries and a CMOS detector array to measure coherence lengths of three diode lasers and a frequency-doubled DPSS laser.
result: Coherence lengths vary among devices but can regularly exceed 10 cm, even for laser pointers exhibiting multimodal behavior.
conclusion: The work offers a practical undergraduate laboratory template and may inspire laser pointer designs that exploit interference effects, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Analog Explorations Of Quantum State Measurement
authors: James P. Crutchfield Benjamin Krawciw
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The awkward disconnect in the postulates of quantum mechanics between the continuous, deterministic, linear, and unitary evolution governed by Schr\"odinger's equation and the discontinuous, stochastic, nonlinear, and nonunitary measurement process has vexed physicists for decades. Intuition from classical mechanics, statistical mechanics, and dynamical systems theory suggests that such a process might be modeled with a nonlinear system of differential equations. We explore such approaches by designing a deterministic model of an ideal projective measurement on a single qubit and constructing an analog computer that simulates it by manipulating voltages in an electrical circuit. The model reduces to Schr\"odinger evolution when no measurement is taking place. During a measurement, a hidden variable that the observer does not resolve selects the outcome, and the model is constructed so that a uniformly distributed hidden variable yields Born-rule frequencies. We do not derive the Born rule; rather, we show that a deterministic dynamical system with no intrinsic noise can implement it. Over 300 trials, the circuit reproduces the ideal model's individual outcomes to within one percent of the decision threshold, and its outcome frequencies match the Born rule to within about 0.02 in probability. These results are a small but provocative step towards modeling quantum measurement with macro-scale machines---a step of interest for both the foundations of physics and the alternatives to digital computing it suggests.
tldr: The paper presents an analog computer circuit that simulates a deterministic model of projective measurement on a qubit, reproducing Born rule statistics without intrinsic noise.
motivation: To address the disconnect between unitary evolution and measurement in quantum mechanics by modeling measurement with deterministic nonlinear dynamics inspired by classical mechanics and dynamical systems theory.
method: Designed a deterministic model of ideal projective measurement on a single qubit with a hidden variable, and built an analog electrical circuit to simulate it; over 300 trials, compared outcomes to the ideal model.
result: The circuit reproduces individual outcomes within 1% of the decision threshold and matches Born rule frequencies to within about 0.02 in probability.
conclusion: Provides a provocative step toward modeling quantum measurement with macro-scale machines, relevant to foundations of physics and alternative computing paradigms.

title: Physics-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement Of Amortized Bayesian Inference Across Physics
authors: Bo Liang, Mingtao Chen, Minghui Du, Ziren Luo, Guohua Wang, Peng Xu, Zhichao Hu, Maxm Pan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Across physics, from the orbits of imaged exoplanets and the matter inside neutron stars to thin films at synchrotrons and cortical neurons, conservation laws, interference, and compensating currents compress the posteriors of precise data into tiny, curved regions where Markov chains need minutes to days. We introduce PhyRSI (physics-guided recursive self-improvement), in which an AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is unknown. It evolves coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations matched to the physics: orbital elements at the best-measured epoch, Fresnel-normalized reflectivity with a chart for each of its multiple solutions, coordinates along which Na+ and K+ currents compensate, a shared neutron-star equation of state that factorizes a 32-dimensional joint analysis, and the time-rescaling symmetry of predator-prey dynamics. In six fields, networks trained once on simulations return 36 posteriors of real observations in seconds, reweighted by the likelihood and agreeing with converged Markov chains about as closely as two independent chains agree with each other. Such posteriors could steer synchrotron film growth and patch-clamp recordings as they run, follow X-ray transients while they are bright, update the dense-matter equation of state as neutron stars are added, and compare physical models across catalogs. Inference can thus be evolved and checked by the physics itself rather than designed by hand for each problem.
tldr: PhyRSI uses an AI agent to write and revise amortized Bayesian inference algorithms tailored to the physics of each problem, producing fast posterior approximations that agree with converged Markov chains.
motivation: Precise physical data compress posteriors into tiny, curved, degenerate regions where MCMC sampling takes minutes to days, so hand-designing problem-specific inference for each field is slow and laborious.
method: An AI agent coupled to a simulator iteratively writes and revises amortized inference networks, scored by importance weights computed from the exact likelihood, while discovering physics-matched coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations.
result: In six fields (exoplanet orbits, neutron-star equations of state, synchrotron reflectivity, ion-channel currents, predator-prey dynamics, and joint EoS analyses), networks trained once on simulations returned 36 posteriors of real observations in seconds, matching converged MCMC chains to within chain-to-chain variation.
conclusion: Inference pipelines can be evolved and validated by the physics itself instead of being hand-designed per problem, enabling real-time posterior updates during experiments and across catalogs.

title: Efficient Convolution-based Nonparaxial Propagation Of Partially Coherent Light
authors: Rafael de la Fuente Herrezuelo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive an efficient formulation for wide-angle propagation of partially coherent light from extended incoherent sources, extending the generalized van Cittert-Zernike Schell (GVS) propagator beyond the paraxial regime with absolute radiometric normalization. Within the Fresnel model, we establish that GVS and the classical paraxial source-PSF convolution are algebraically equivalent, explicitly deriving the corresponding source inversion, magnification, and absolute radiometric normalization. The resulting separation of mapped source and coherent pupil response enables wide-angle convolution in direction-cosine coordinates. Within a physically motivated diffracted-radiance formulation, this far-field convolution is exact for incoherent plane-wave mixtures. The same power prescription also relates delta-correlated source statistics to Lambertian radiance and hemispherical emitted power. At finite distances, we use a common incident curvature and approximate the source contributions by shifting and weighting a single coherent monitor response in direction-cosine coordinates. The differentiable formulation supports gradient-based inverse design of diffractive elements and metasurfaces represented by scalar pupils. Examples reveal geometric distortion and irradiance fall-off missed by the paraxial models and demonstrate wide-angle beam shaping at finite distances. A benchmark shows orders of magnitude faster evaluation than source-by-source propagation with a common error tolerance.
tldr: The paper derives an efficient convolution-based formulation for wide-angle (nonparaxial) propagation of partially coherent light from extended incoherent sources, extending the generalized van Cittert-Zernike Schell propagator with absolute radiometric normalization.
motivation: Existing propagators for partially coherent light are largely restricted to the paraxial regime, so wide-angle beam shaping and inverse design of diffractive elements lack an efficient and radiometrically normalized propagation model.
method: The authors show algebraic equivalence between the GVS propagator and the classical paraxial source-PSF convolution within the Fresnel model, derive source inversion, magnification and radiometric normalization, and express the wide-angle problem as a convolution in direction-cosine coordinates; a differentiable formulation is used for gradient-based inverse design.
result: The formulation yields orders-of-magnitude faster evaluation than source-by-source propagation at a common error tolerance and reveals geometric distortion and irradiance fall-off missed by paraxial models, enabling wide-angle beam shaping at finite distances.
conclusion: The work provides a practical, differentiable and radiometrically calibrated framework for nonparaxial propagation of partially coherent light, useful for designing diffractive optical elements and metasurfaces.

title: Recovering From Averages: An Inverse Problem Perspective On Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
authors: Tina Torabi, Cheuk Hin Ho, Christoph Ortner, Ruo Ning Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate the potential energy surface of atomistic systems from quantum-mechanical reference data and enable molecular simulation at near-ab-initio accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Since they are fitted to total energies and forces, it is not obvious what is estimated: the total energy or the many-body potentials from which it is assembled. Mathematically, this can be formulated as a question whether a function can be recovered from averages of its values over random clusters. We study it for a linear model of fixed correlation order in simplified statistical setting. We show that, in the population limit, the potential is identifiable in a natural weighted Sobolev space, and derive finite-sample recovery guarantees. Numerical experiments for pair, three-body, and four-body models support the theory.
tldr: The paper casts machine-learning interatomic potentials as an inverse problem of recovering a many-body potential function from averages over random clusters, proving identifiability and finite-sample recovery guarantees in a linear fixed-order model.
motivation: MLIPs are trained on total energies and forces, so it is unclear whether the fitted model recovers the underlying many-body potential or only reproduces aggregate quantities; the authors seek a rigorous statistical answer.
method: They formulate recovery of a function from averages of its values over random clusters in a simplified statistical setting with a linear model of fixed correlation order, prove identifiability in a weighted Sobolev space, and derive finite-sample error bounds, supported by numerical experiments for pair, three-body and four-body models.
result: In the population limit the potential is identifiable in a natural weighted Sobolev space, and explicit finite-sample recovery guarantees are obtained and confirmed numerically.
conclusion: A mathematical foundation is provided for what MLIPs actually learn, clarifying identifiability and sample complexity of many-body potential reconstruction.

title: Categorification Of The Reduced Stated ${\rm SL}_n$-skein Algebras Of Polygons
authors: Zhihao Wang Min Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be the reduced stated [MATH]-skein algebra of a polygon with [MATH] boundary punctures ([MATH]). Building on the quantum cluster algebra structure of [MATH] established by Cao and the authors, and on the monoidal category [MATH] of finite-dimensional modules over the quantum affine algebra [MATH] introduced by Kashiwara, Kim, Oh and Park, where [MATH] is the Garside element of [MATH], we give a monoidal categorification of [MATH]. As a consequence, [MATH] has a basis with positive structure constants. A key role is played by the subalgebra [MATH] spanned by the stated [MATH]-webs whose [MATH] edge weights are zero. We show that [MATH] is a quantum cluster algebra whose seed coincides with the Kashiwara--Kim--Oh--Park seed of [MATH]. Hence it is the quantum Grothendieck ring of a monoidal localization, at the frozen modules, of a subcategory of [MATH] with the same simple objects, and a quantization of the braid variety [MATH]. The whole algebra [MATH] is a skew Laurent extension of [MATH] in [MATH] frozen variables.
tldr: The paper constructs a monoidal categorification of the reduced stated SL_n-skein algebra of polygons using categories of modules over a quantum affine algebra, showing it is a quantum cluster algebra with positive structure constants.
motivation: Skein algebras of surfaces have rich quantum cluster algebra structures, and the authors aim to lift this algebraic structure to a categorical (monoidal) level in the spirit of Kashiwara-Kim-Oh-Park's work on quantum affine algebras.
method: They build on the quantum cluster algebra structure of the reduced stated skein algebra and on the monoidal category of finite-dimensional modules over the quantum affine algebra truncated by the Garside element, identifying the subalgebra of webs with zero edge weights as a quantum cluster algebra matching the Kashiwara-Kim-Oh-Park seed.
result: A monoidal categorification is obtained, yielding a basis with positive structure constants; the zero-edge-weight subalgebra is realized as the quantum Grothendieck ring of a monoidal localization and as a quantization of a braid variety, with the full algebra a skew Laurent extension in frozen variables.
conclusion: The reduced stated SL_n-skein algebras of polygons admit monoidal categorifications, linking skein theory, quantum cluster algebras, and representations of quantum affine algebras.

title: Inverse Scattering For The One-dimensional Discrete Schr\"odinger Operator: A Computational Perspective
authors: Basant Lal Sharma Peter C. Gibson
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit inverse scattering for the one-dimensional discrete Schr\"odinger operator with compactly supported perturbation. We consider a computational perspective, adapted to the case of a digitally sampled reflection coefficient, to determine the perturbation in the form of a Jacobi matrix, including a computation of the length of the smallest interval supporting the perturbation. A new representation of scattering data in terms of orthogonal polynomials underpins the computational results. A key technical role is played by polynomials on the circle constructed from pairs of successive orthogonal polynomials on the line. The inverse algorithm is demonstrated on numerical examples.
tldr: This paper develops a computational approach to inverse scattering for the one-dimensional discrete Schrödinger operator with compactly supported perturbation.
motivation: The authors revisit inverse scattering for discrete Schrödinger operators from a numerical perspective, aiming to reconstruct a Jacobi matrix from a digitally sampled reflection coefficient.
method: The method uses a new representation of scattering data via orthogonal polynomials, including polynomials on the circle constructed from successive orthogonal polynomials on the line, and computes the support length of the perturbation.
result: The inverse algorithm is demonstrated on numerical examples, reconstructing the perturbation and determining the smallest interval supporting it.
conclusion: The work provides a practical computational framework for discrete inverse scattering, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Balanced Boolean Functions From Sparse Niho-Type Permutation Polynomials: Few-Valued Walsh Spectra And Applications
authors: Jun Zhang Chenxu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study balanced Boolean functions parameterized by two-to-one mappings of the forms [MATH] and [MATH], where [MATH] is a sparse permutation polynomial with generalized Niho-type exponents. First, for [MATH] with [MATH] even, we determine the complete four-valued Walsh distribution of the balanced Boolean function parameterized by [MATH], where [MATH]. We then generalize a permutation polynomial studied by Gupta and Sharma to the parameterized family [MATH] over [MATH]. We prove that [MATH] is a permutation polynomial if and only if either [MATH], or [MATH] and [MATH] has no root in [MATH]. Moreover, the number of admissible parameters is [MATH] when [MATH] is even and [MATH] when [MATH] is odd. Thus, admissible parameters exist for every [MATH], and approximately one-third of the elements of [MATH] yield permutation polynomials. For every admissible parameter [MATH], we determine the complete Walsh distribution of the balanced Boolean function [MATH] parameterized by [MATH] and prove that this distribution is independent of [MATH]. For [MATH], these functions have the five-valued Walsh spectrum [MATH], while for [MATH] the spectrum degenerates to four values. As applications, their supports yield projective minimal binary five-weight codes, sets with five hyperplane intersection numbers, and regular cubelike Cayley graphs with six distinct eigenvalues. Finally, for mappings of the form [MATH], we construct an infinite family of balanced Boolean functions with simple explicit trace representations.
tldr: The paper constructs and analyzes balanced Boolean functions from sparse Niho-type permutation polynomials, deriving few-valued Walsh spectra and applications to codes and Cayley graphs.
motivation: Balanced Boolean functions with few-valued Walsh spectra are important in classical cryptography and coding theory, motivating the study of new permutation-polynomial-based constructions.
method: The authors characterize permutation polynomials of generalized Niho type, count admissible parameters, and compute complete Walsh distributions for the resulting balanced Boolean functions.
result: They obtain four- and five-valued Walsh spectra, prove independence of the spectrum from the parameter, and derive projective minimal binary five-weight codes and related combinatorial structures.
conclusion: The work extends classical Boolean-function constructions and provides new explicit families with useful spectral and coding properties, but it is purely classical and not connected to quantum information.

title: Structure-Preserving Model Reduction Of Metriplectic Systems Via Oblique Projections And Block Structure
authors: Cecilia Pagliantini Andrea Benvenuti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metriplectic systems combine conservative and dissipative dynamics and are characterized by energy conservation and entropy production. The degeneracy conditions underlying these properties are generally not preserved by standard projection-based model order reduction. We develop two structure-preserving reduction strategies. The first enforces degeneracy conditions through oblique projections and combines gradient-preserving and matrix empirical interpolation for hyper-reduction. The second constructs reduced bases adapted to available operator block structure, preserving degeneracy without online oblique corrections. We establish sufficient conditions for preserving the Jacobi identity and derive a priori error estimates. Numerical tests on benchmark problems demonstrate accuracy, thermodynamic consistency, and computational efficiency.
tldr: The paper develops structure-preserving model order reduction methods for classical metriplectic systems using oblique projections and block-structure-adapted reduced bases.
motivation: Standard projection-based model reduction destroys the degeneracy conditions that guarantee energy conservation and entropy production in metriplectic systems, so structure-preserving reduced models are needed.
method: Two reduction strategies are proposed: one enforces degeneracy via oblique projections with gradient-preserving and matrix empirical interpolation hyper-reduction, and the other constructs reduced bases adapted to operator block structure to preserve degeneracy without online oblique corrections.
result: The authors establish sufficient conditions for preserving the Jacobi identity and derive a priori error estimates; numerical benchmark tests demonstrate accuracy, thermodynamic consistency, and computational efficiency.
conclusion: The proposed methods provide accurate and thermodynamically consistent reduced-order models for metriplectic systems, but the work is classical numerical model reduction and does not address quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Pcc: Proof-Carrying Credentials For Enhanced Anonymity And Post-Quantum Delegation
authors: Zixuan Wang, Zheng Tianyu, Yuan Lu, Bin Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delegatable Anonymous Credentials (DACs) support anonymous exercise of authority delegated through intermediaries, as in DeFi credit delegation. Existing DACs require holders to possess and process chain-shaped lineage material for presentation. We call this limitation : presentation cost grows with delegation depth, while holder-visible topology can enable lineage-based vetoes, strategic disintermediation, and de facto censorship. We formalize the privacy dimension as (EDA), a leakage-parametrized two-observer notion combining verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology obliviousness. We give simulation and indistinguishability formulations over paths with identical allowed holder leakage. Our framework, (PCC), addresses both limitations by replacing the explicit chain with a recursively updated proof-carrying state via Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC). PCC makes presentation independent of delegation depth and hides topology beyond permitted leakage, while preserving restricted delegation and expressive presentation. Unlike pairing-based constant-size DACs, PCC is hardness-agnostic and admits a post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM using transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures. On consumer-grade hardware, the Halo2 instantiation keeps a constant 7.344\,KB verifier-facing proof with 35--36\,ms verification across all tested depths. The 128-bit Plonky2 instantiation keeps a constant 157.9\,KB proof with 3.8\,ms verification across depths [MATH], at 1.03\,s per delegation step. These results demonstrate practical depth-independent presentation and holder-side topology hiding.
tldr: The paper introduces PCC, a proof-carrying credential framework for delegatable anonymous credentials that hides delegation topology and achieves depth-independent presentation, including post-quantum-compatible instantiations.
motivation: Existing delegatable anonymous credentials require holders to process chain-shaped lineage material, causing presentation cost to grow with delegation depth and leaking holder-visible topology that can enable censorship or strategic disintermediation.
method: The authors formalize a privacy notion called EDA and replace explicit delegation chains with a recursively updated proof-carrying state using Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation, with Halo2 and Plonky2 instantiations.
result: The Halo2 instantiation yields a constant 7.344 KB proof with 35–36 ms verification across depths, while the Plonky2 instantiation yields a constant 157.9 KB proof with 3.8 ms verification at about 1.03 s per delegation step.
conclusion: PCC demonstrates practical depth-independent presentation and holder-side topology hiding, and it supports a post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM.

title: Mjolnir: Finding And Reproducing Vulnerabilities In Root-of-Trust Firmware And Rtl With Project-Grounded Agents
authors: Collin Macdonald, Carl Lundin, Stephen Herwig, Miguel Osorio, Timothy Trippel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A root of trust (RoT) anchors secure boot and attestation for the system above it, so a bug in RoT firmware or hardware undermines every layer that trusts it. LLM agents now find real vulnerabilities in general-purpose software, but RoT code presents two challenges. First, many security-relevant bugs depend on project-specific trust boundaries and fault-injection countermeasures rather than generic vulnerability patterns, and may cause no crash. Second, without RoT hardware, agents must exercise RoT inputs through the project's own hardware model, mocks, or RTL testbenches. We present Mjolnir, an agentic pipeline that supplies each project's threat model and design conventions to discovery and skeptical review agents, and reproduces surviving findings as proof-of-concept tests in the project's own toolchain. We evaluate Mjolnir on six firmware and RTL targets in Caliptra, OpenTitan, and OpenPRoT. On Caliptra's runtime firmware, it reaches 83.3%-100% precision across three models under blind expert labeling, including 100% on Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 66.7%-78.6% for four single-agent baselines on the same model. On 34 known security-relevant bugs in Caliptra's core firmware fixed after the models' training cutoffs, it finds 10 with Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 7 for the best baseline, and 17 with Gemini 4 Argon versus 12. Across our evaluation scans, maintainers have confirmed 64 of Mjolnir's findings as previously unknown security-relevant bugs: 37 across three models on Caliptra's runtime firmware and 27 across single scans of the other five targets.
tldr: Mjolnir is an LLM-agent pipeline that discovers and reproduces security vulnerabilities in root-of-trust firmware and RTL by grounding agents in each project's threat model, design conventions, and native verification toolchains.
motivation: Roots of trust underpin secure boot and attestation, but their bugs depend on project-specific trust boundaries and fault-injection countermeasures rather than generic patterns, and evaluating them without hardware requires exercising inputs through mocks and RTL testbenches.
method: The pipeline feeds per-project threat models and design conventions to discovery and skeptical-review agents, then converts surviving findings into proof-of-concept tests within the project's own toolchain; it is evaluated on six firmware and RTL targets across Caliptra, OpenTitan, and OpenPRoT with blind expert labeling and comparison against single-agent baselines.
result: On Caliptra runtime firmware Mjolnir achieves 83.3%-100% precision across three models (100% with Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 66.7%-78.6% for baselines), finds 10 of 34 post-cutoff known bugs versus 7 for the best baseline, and maintainers confirmed 64 previously unknown security-relevant findings.
conclusion: Project-grounded agentic analysis substantially improves vulnerability discovery and reproduction in root-of-trust firmware and hardware, with high precision validated by maintainers.

title: Coding Length And Optimal Power Allocation In Correlated Block Fading
authors: Huazhong Zhao Haoran Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A codeword spans a fixed number of correlated Gaussian fading blocks. The receiver knows the gains and the transmitter knows only their law. At fixed average signal-to-noise ratio, we require the decoding error probability to decay exponentially with the number of receive antennas. When does outage predict the achievable rate? If block length grows faster than the number of antennas, outage gives the limiting optimal rate. If both grow to infinity at a fixed positive ratio of block length to array size, outage strictly overestimates the limiting rate. We determine the critical ratio above which positive rates are possible. For sufficiently large finite ratios, we find the exact limiting rate over all codes satisfying a total energy constraint on each codeword. The leading rate loss is inversely proportional to the ratio. Its coefficient depends on Gaussian channel dispersion at the most likely fade causing outage and on how quickly the outage rate decreases as the required error exponent increases. In the long-block limit, equal power loses rate on every window of three or more blocks under stationary first-order autoregressive fading with positive lag-one correlation. In a different three-block channel with identical marginal gains, tightening the reliability requirement first makes it optimal to leave the middle block unused and later to use it again.
tldr: This paper analyzes classical coding over correlated Gaussian block-fading channels, deriving when outage predicts the achievable rate and characterizing optimal power allocation under finite blocklength constraints.
motivation: The authors aim to clarify the relationship between outage capacity and achievable rates when codewords span multiple correlated fading blocks and block length scales with the number of receive antennas.
method: They study error exponents and limiting rates for correlated block-fading channels with receiver channel knowledge and transmitter knowledge only of the fading law, deriving critical block-length-to-antenna ratios and exact asymptotic rate losses.
result: Outage predicts the limiting optimal rate only when block length grows faster than antenna count; at fixed positive ratio, outage overestimates the rate. The leading rate loss scales inversely with this ratio and depends on Gaussian channel dispersion at the dominant outage fade.
conclusion: The work provides finite-blocklength rate characterizations and shows that equal power allocation can be suboptimal over windows of three or more blocks under correlated autoregressive fading.

title: Do Alice And Bob Dream Of The Oracle? Wishful Cryptanalysis
authors: Guoxiao Liu, Keting Jia, Hongbo Yu, Zongyue Wang, Tianshuo Cong, Junfeng Fan, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For two millennia, offense and defense have forged cryptographic security boundaries. Tools automated calculation and search, while humans drove discovery. Foundation models now mark a shift from automated computation to intelligent scientific discovery. Because cryptanalysis rests on exact mathematical definitions and immediately executable truth, it offers a proving ground for autonomous intelligence to move past security reliant on scarce human attention and explore structures beyond human working memory. Unguided models stall between two opposite traps: authority hallucination, where they surrender whenever prior literature declares a route blocked, and reasoning hallucination, where they produce subtle, unverifiable flaws. Closed platforms and generic agent loops further impede sustained open inquiry. We introduce wishful cryptanalysis, a harness-agnostic methodology that pairs constructive optimism against entrenched assumptions with blinded, zero-import verification against error. Agents first compress reduced-scale theory within provisioned compute so live witnesses certify their mathematics automatically. They then co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, and climb parameter ladders toward high-round theory. Applied across frontier open-weight and proprietary models with minimal human intervention beyond targets and compute, this paradigm yielded novel attack techniques and thirteen verifiable practical results across Keccak (SHA-3) and AES. These include breaking a fifteen-year-open public challenge and closing longstanding practical gaps, released alongside an early-preview open-source workbench (agent-framework). Extending Kerckhoffs's principle into the AI era, we envision an Open Oracle, an open and auditable public infrastructure that frees cryptographers to legislate security goals, challenge assumptions, distill theory, and co-design resilient standards.
tldr: The paper introduces 'wishful cryptanalysis', an LLM-agent methodology for autonomously discovering attacks on symmetric primitives, demonstrated by 13 practical results against Keccak (SHA-3) and AES, including a break of a 15-year-open public challenge.
motivation: Foundation models shift cryptanalysis from automated computation toward autonomous scientific discovery, but unguided models suffer from authority hallucination (deferring to literature declaring a route blocked) and reasoning hallucination (producing unverifiable flaws), while closed platforms and generic agent loops impede sustained open inquiry.
method: A harness-agnostic framework pairs constructive optimism against entrenched assumptions with blinded, zero-import verification: agents first compress reduced-scale theory under provisioned compute so live witnesses certify their mathematics automatically, then co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, and climb parameter ladders toward high-round theory with minimal human intervention.
result: Applied across frontier open-weight and proprietary models, the paradigm produced novel attack techniques and thirteen verifiable practical results on Keccak (SHA-3) and AES, including breaking a fifteen-year-open public challenge and closing longstanding practical gaps, released with an early-preview open-source workbench.
conclusion: The authors propose extending Kerckhoffs's principle into the AI era via an 'Open Oracle' — open, auditable public infrastructure for cryptanalysis — and argue that AI-driven attack discovery should reshape how cryptographers set security goals and co-design resilient standards.

title: Hardness Of Algorithmic Kadison-Singer Problem From Approximate Hypergraph Colouring
authors: Danny Vagnozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2015, Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava published a solution of a strong form of a conjecture by Weaver implying a positive answer to the Kadison-Singer problem - an open question of interest to several fields of pure and applied mathematics. Specifically, they proved that for all [MATH] and finite lists of vectors whose Euclidean norm is at most [MATH] and whose outer products sum to the identity matrix, there exists a signed sum of these outer products whose operator norm is at most [MATH]. Since then, significant effort has been put into understanding the algorithmic side of the Kadison-Singer problem; that is, the task of actually finding a signing resulting in a matrix with operator norm at most [MATH] for some fixed constant [MATH]. The first hardness results for this problem were proven independently by Spielman and Zhang [APPROX'22] and by Jourdan, Macgregor and Sun [ISAAC'23]. In this short note, we prove that there exist values of [MATH] arbitrarily close to [MATH] such that it is NP-hard to distinguish indexed families of vectors for which there is a signed sum with operator norm equal to [MATH] from those for which every signed sum has operator norm at least [MATH]. This improves on the previous best bound by Spielman and Zhang. Our proof borrows significant ideas from the above mentioned hardness results, by adapting them to a reduction from the problem of approximating hypergraph colouring in the sense of promise constraint satisfaction problems.
tldr: This short note proves improved NP-hardness bounds for the algorithmic Kadison-Singer problem via a reduction from approximate hypergraph colouring.
motivation: The algorithmic side of the Kadison-Singer/Weaver solution is important for discrepancy theory and approximation algorithms, and prior hardness results left room for stronger inapproximability bounds.
method: The author adapts existing hardness reductions and reduces from approximating hypergraph colouring in the promise constraint satisfaction framework to the problem of finding signed sums with bounded operator norm.
result: For constants arbitrarily close to a limiting value, it is NP-hard to distinguish vector families admitting a signing with operator norm exactly that value from those where every signing has operator norm at least a larger constant.
conclusion: The work improves the best known hardness bound for algorithmic Kadison-Singer, but it is a pure mathematics/complexity result with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Adaptive Collective Decision-Making In Signed Networks
authors: Vishnudatta Thota, Aditi Saxena, Twinkle Tripathy, Vaibhav Srivastava
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collective decision-making often unfolds in networks where cooperation and antagonism coexist. Such signed interactions arise in social, biological, and robotic systems, and can lead to qualitatively different collective outcomes: consensus, polarization, or clustering. Existing signed network models typically explain these outcomes separately, leaving open how they can emerge within a single dynamical framework. Here, we introduce a generalized Laplacian flow for bi-partitioned signed networks, a class of networks that allows cooperative and antagonistic interactions both within and across two prescribed groups. The proposed model includes an adaptive social effort state, interpreted as a leaky memory of persistent signed network disagreement, which enables bounded and nontrivial steady-states beyond classical signed Laplacian flows. We derive conditions that determine whether the network reaches consensus, polarization, or clustering based on the spectral structure of the generalized Laplacian and effective resistance matrices. The framework applies beyond structurally balanced, weakly balanced, and quasi-structurally balanced networks, and reveals how changes in signed interaction strengths can shift a network between collective decision regimes. We validate the theory on stochastic block model networks, a judicial voting network, and a U.S. senate bill co-sponsorship network. Altogether, our results provide a structural and dynamical account of how mixed cooperative and antagonistic relationships shape emergent collective behaviors.
tldr: The paper introduces a generalized Laplacian flow with an adaptive social-effort state for bi-partitioned signed networks, deriving spectral conditions for consensus, polarization, and clustering.
motivation: Signed networks with mixed cooperative and antagonistic interactions produce qualitatively different collective outcomes that existing models explain only in isolation, so the authors seek a single dynamical framework encompassing all regimes.
method: They extend signed Laplacian flow with a leaky-memory adaptive effort variable and characterize steady states via the spectral structure of generalized Laplacian and effective resistance matrices, testing on stochastic block models and two real signed networks.
result: The model yields bounded nontrivial steady states beyond classical signed Laplacian flows, and spectral conditions predict whether consensus, polarization, or clustering emerges, including for networks beyond structural or weak balance.
conclusion: Mixed cooperative-antagonistic interactions admit a unified structural-dynamical account of collective decision regimes, with interaction strengths acting as control knobs between regimes.

title: Conductivity Of Electrolyte Solutions: Self-consistent Debye-H\"{u}ckel-Onsager Theory
authors: Nikolai Kalikin Yury Budkov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study presents a novel approach to addressing the limitations in understanding the behavior of charged particles in solutions. The approach is based on the development of the Self-Consistent Debye-H\"uckel-Onsager (SCDHO) theory, which integrates the effects of non-local charge distributions using a Slater-type charge form factor model. This results in a modified Coulomb potential at short distances, unlike traditional approaches such as the classical Debye-H\"uckel-Onsager theory. The proposed method relies on explicit expressions derived from gradients of local chemical potentials rooted in classical Density Functional Theory (DFT) and the Ornstein-Zernike formalism for correlation functions. Our theoretical framework enables the derivation of analytic equations that describe both correlation (aka relaxation) and electrophoretic contributions to total electric conductivity. Within the established theoretical framework, the model of smeared charges with Slater-type charge form factors provides an accurate predictive tool that can be applied to a wide range of ion valences, concentrations, and temperatures, including both aqueous and non-aqueous electrolyte solutions.
tldr: A self-consistent Debye-Hückel-Onsager theory with Slater-type charge form factors is developed to predict the electrical conductivity of aqueous and non-aqueous electrolyte solutions.
motivation: Classical Debye-Hückel-Onsager theory fails to accurately describe ion behavior at short distances and across wide ranges of valence, concentration, and temperature, motivating a refined treatment of non-local charge distributions.
method: The authors combine classical Density Functional Theory gradients of local chemical potentials with the Ornstein-Zernike correlation-function formalism, introducing a smeared Slater-type charge form factor that modifies the short-range Coulomb potential, and derive analytic expressions for relaxation and electrophoretic conductivity contributions.
result: The SCDHO framework yields closed-form analytic equations for correlation and electrophoretic contributions to total conductivity and is claimed to predict conductivity accurately across ion valences, concentrations, and temperatures in both aqueous and non-aqueous solvents.
conclusion: Smeared-charge SCDHO theory offers a practical predictive tool for electrolyte conductivity, extending classical theory beyond its short-range limitations.

title: A Posteriori Estimates For Inverse Evolutionary Problems
authors: Sergey Repin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper is focused on a posteriori error analysis of evolutionary problems, which are ill-posed in the sense of Hadamard. They may have no solutions and respective approximations may be highly unstable. For these problems, the a posteriori error estimation concept applicable to well-posed problems is not valid and requires a significant reformulation. A posteriori estimates of the functional type provide the basis for addressing this issue. They generate computable quantities that estimate the distance between a function (approximate solution to the inverse problem) and exact solution of a "close" well-posed initial boundary value problem associated with the same differential equation. The solution of this close problem exactly satisfies one part of the imposed conditions and the others are satisfied approximately with the accuracy [MATH]. This idea is elaborated for several evolutionary problems generated by the reaction-convection-diffusion equation: backward parabolic problem, problem with non-local time conditions, Cauchy parabolic problem, and parameter(s) identification problem. The estimates derived not only control the accuracy of approximate solutions, but also suggest a unified approach to calculating them numerically.
tldr: The paper develops a posteriori functional-type error estimates for ill-posed evolutionary inverse problems governed by reaction-convection-diffusion equations, including backward parabolic, non-local time-condition, Cauchy, and parameter-identification problems.
motivation: Classical a posteriori error estimation theory assumes well-posedness, so it breaks down for Hadamard-ill-posed evolutionary inverse problems where solutions may not exist and approximations are unstable; a reformulation is needed.
method: Functional a posteriori estimates are constructed by comparing an approximate solution to the exact solution of a 'close' well-posed initial-boundary value problem sharing the same differential equation, where some conditions hold exactly and others only to accuracy epsilon.
result: The approach yields computable quantities that bound the distance between approximate and exact solutions for several classes of evolutionary inverse problems and additionally provides a unified numerical framework.
conclusion: Functional a posteriori estimation offers a viable and unifying route to error control for ill-posed evolutionary inverse problems, extending standard estimation concepts beyond the well-posed setting.

title: Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping Via Android Camera2 Metadata
authors: Guangyuan Ji, Wenjing Wang, Bingsheng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To prevent motion sensors from acting as covert microphones, Android 12+ caps SensorManager gyroscope and accelerometer rates at 200 Hz by default, requires HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS for higher rates, and throttles sensors back to 200 Hz when the microphone toggle is off. We show that Android's Camera2 subsystem bypasses these defenses. During an active Camera2 session, Camera HAL stabilization pipelines record high-rate gyroscope measurements and export them via vendor CaptureResult metadata. Loudspeaker speech excites chassis vibrations that couple into this path. Across 50 smartphones (2020-2026) from 10 vendors, 37 expose gyroscope metadata via Camera2, and 26 exceed 200 Hz--including six flagship models at 800-1000 Hz, double SensorManager's 400-500 Hz ceiling. This channel requires neither RECORD_AUDIO nor HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS and defeats privacy switches: turning off the microphone toggle does not throttle metadata, and turning off the camera toggle blanks only video frames while 800-1000 Hz metadata keeps streaming. To build a zero-profiling attack that generalizes to unseen phones, we introduce Source-to-Leakage Learning (S2L). Prior attacks train on real sensor traces, entangling speech with a specific phone's mechanical resonances and sampling rate. S2L decouples speech content from hardware acoustics using a physics-constrained forward simulator. Trained exclusively on simulated leakage without target-phone traces, our universal recognizer CamEar achieves 52.1% mean word accuracy (up to 61.8%) and 74.3% character accuracy (up to 80.7%) across the six 800-1000 Hz phones.
