Finally, we solve the inverse problem of identifying the three Windkessel parameters of the outlet from synthetic data, recovering them with errors of about 0.3% from deliberately wrong initial values. Residual biases in the local pressure field and the need to test robustness to noisy clinical data remain open, but the results support PINNs as complementary tools for meshless hemodynamics and patient-specific digital twins.
tldr: A meshless physics-informed neural network framework solves 3D pulsatile blood flow in patient-specific pulmonary artery geometries with Windkessel (RCR) outlet boundary conditions, including inverse identification of the outlet parameters.
motivation: Mesh-based CFD for cardiovascular flow is accurate but computationally expensive and requires complex meshing workflows, limiting clinical translation; PINNs offer a meshless alternative that embeds the governing equations directly into training.
method: The authors decompose pressure into a time-dependent basal part and a spatially varying part, add an initial condition and gauge for the Windkessel ODE, impose a global mass-balance constraint, and use a periodic Fourier embedding of time; the framework is validated on 2D canonical channels and then applied to a patient-specific right pulmonary artery, with the inverse problem of recovering three Windkessel parameters solved from synthetic data.
result: The framework reproduces outlet flow, mean pressure, and velocity and dynamic pressure fields to errors on the order of the data resolution, and recovers the three Windkessel parameters with about 0.3% error starting from deliberately wrong initial values.
conclusion: PINNs appear to be viable complementary tools for meshless patient-specific hemodynamics and digital twins, though residual biases in the local pressure field and robustness to noisy clinical data remain open issues.

title: Linear Convergence Of Adaptive Accelerated Gradient Methods: A Unified Framework
authors: Ming Yan Weihe Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a unified Lyapunov framework for adaptive accelerated gradient methods on smooth, strongly convex objectives. Conditions on local curvature, stepsize ratios, and coefficient variation ensure eventual linear convergence without assuming stepsize convergence. We verify these conditions for specified AdaNAG-G, smooth unconstrained AC-FGM, and AdaAGM policies and use them to design VC-FG and CC-FG. The verified adaptive main iterations require neither global smoothness nor strong-convexity parameters and avoid restart and backtracking. The framework also sharpens a fixed-step FISTA/NAG-type bound. Experiments on four smooth, strongly convex problem families illustrate complementary performance of the new methods.
tldr: The paper presents a unified Lyapunov framework that guarantees eventual linear convergence of adaptive accelerated gradient methods on smooth, strongly convex objectives without requiring stepsize convergence.
motivation: Adaptive accelerated gradient methods often lack convergence guarantees because stepsizes and momentum coefficients vary, so the authors aim to identify general conditions that still ensure linear convergence.
method: They derive conditions on local curvature, stepsize ratios, and coefficient variation within a Lyapunov analysis, verify them for AdaNAG-G, AC-FGM, and AdaAGM, and use them to design two new schemes, VC-FG and CC-FG.
result: The verified adaptive iterations attain linear convergence without global smoothness or strong-convexity parameters and without restart or backtracking, and the framework also sharpens a fixed-step FISTA/NAG-type bound, supported by experiments on four strongly convex problem families.
conclusion: A unified Lyapunov-based framework explains and extends linear convergence of adaptive accelerated gradient methods, yielding practical new algorithms with competitive empirical performance.

title: Exploring Early Vulnerability Analysis Via Automatic Identification Of Vulnerability-Introducing Commits
authors: Weiliang Qi, Shu Wang, Youpeng Li, Ela Guo, Xinda Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developing effective vulnerability analysis techniques requires high-quality datasets that capture how vulnerabilities appear and evolve in real software codebase. Existing datasets, however, typically label as vulnerable only the code immediately preceding vulnerability-fixing commits (VFCs), overlooking the earlier versions in which vulnerabilities were first introduced and subsequently evolved. This practice limits both dataset coverage and our understanding of whether current detectors can identify vulnerabilities during their early, latent stages. In this paper, we present three manually annotated datasets of vulnerability-introducing commits (VICs) based on recent CVEs and widely used open-source projects. We further propose D-SZZ, a data state-aware VIC identification framework that analyzes security-fixing patterns and performs vulnerability scope slicing to recover the semantics implied by a fix. Experimental results demonstrate that D-SZZ outperforms existing SZZ and LLM-based baselines in identifying VICs. In addition, we evaluate six representative vulnerability detectors and find that models trained only on pre-VFC code struggle with original vulnerabilities, while incorporating early-stage samples improves detection performance. We also show that D-SZZ improves downstream vulnerable-version identification, and use it to uncover 16 inaccurate affected-version records in the NVD, all of which were officially confirmed and updated.
tldr: The paper introduces manually annotated datasets of vulnerability-introducing commits and a data-state-aware framework (D-SZZ) for identifying them earlier than vulnerability-fixing commits.
motivation: Existing vulnerability datasets label only code immediately preceding fixing commits, missing the earlier versions where vulnerabilities were first introduced, which limits dataset coverage and understanding of detectors' ability to catch latent vulnerabilities.
method: The authors build three manually annotated VIC datasets from recent CVEs and popular open-source projects, and propose D-SZZ, which analyzes security-fixing patterns and performs vulnerability scope slicing to recover fix semantics.
result: D-SZZ outperforms SZZ and LLM-based baselines in identifying VICs; detectors trained only on pre-fix code struggle with original vulnerabilities while early-stage samples improve detection, and D-SZZ also improves vulnerable-version identification, uncovering 16 NVD records later officially confirmed.
conclusion: Early vulnerability-introducing commits provide valuable signal for dataset construction and detector training, and automated VIC identification can also correct downstream vulnerability-version records.

title: Extracting Next Generation Access Control Policies From Natural Language Using LLMs: An Intermediate-Representation Approach With Back-Translation Verification
authors: Ayesha Habib, Huixiang Zhang, Waiz Haider
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organizations write access-control rules in natural language, but NIST's Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) needs them as a formal policy graph. Large language models (LLMs) can automate this translation, but their output can break the format, add rules the text does not state, or drop conditions. We present NGAC-IR, which follows model-driven engineering (MDE). First, the LLM fills in an intermediate representation (IR), a JSON template that records who may, must or must not do what, on which resource and under which condition; a grammar keeps the output within this template. Second, a compiler that uses no LLM converts the IR into an NGAC policy graph and links each rule to its source sentence. Third, a back-translation check writes each rule in English and asks an LLM whether the source sentence states it. On four public datasets, all outputs could be compiled, compared with 95.5% without the grammar, and 95.7% were faithful to their sentence. NGAC-IR outperforms two published methods on all four datasets: the LLM-based Code4Policy in exact match and faithfulness, and the rule-based extractor of Abdelgawad et al. in rule type. The back-translation check sent 10.5% of sentences to human review and found 26 of the 31 errors. To test enforcement, we deployed the compiled policies in NIST's Policy Machine: they gave the expected decision for all 390 access requests, and the tested obligations were carried out. On one local server with open-weight models, all 714 sentences take about 20 minutes and 0.35 kWh, at zero API cost.
tldr: NGAC-IR uses an LLM-filled JSON intermediate representation plus a deterministic compiler and LLM-based back-translation check to convert natural-language access-control rules into NIST NGAC policy graphs.
motivation: Organizations state access-control rules in natural language while NGAC requires a formal policy graph, and direct LLM translation can violate format, hallucinate rules, or drop conditions.
method: A grammar-constrained LLM populates a JSON IR recording who may/must/must-not do what on which resource under which condition; a non-LLM compiler converts the IR into an NGAC policy graph with sentence-level provenance; a back-translation step regenerates English rules and asks an LLM to verify them against source sentences.
result: All outputs compiled (vs 95.5% without grammar), 95.7% were faithful, the approach beat Code4Policy and a rule-based extractor on four datasets, the back-translation check routed 10.5% of sentences to humans and caught 26 of 31 errors, and deployed policies gave expected decisions on all 390 access requests.
conclusion: Structured intermediate representations with verification make LLM-based policy extraction reliable and enforceable, running on open-weight models at ~0.35 kWh for 714 sentences with zero API cost.

title: Subverting Tool Arguments: Defense-Evading Metadata Poisoning In Llm Agents
authors: Shih-Chieh Dai, Xinyu Sun, Haichuan Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhong, Guanhong Tao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks hijack an LLM agent's workflow through malicious instructions embedded in retrieved external content. The growing adoption of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) exposes another attack surface: tool descriptions supplied by third-party MCP servers. Attackers can manipulate this metadata to induce malicious argument generation during tool calls. The challenge is to ensure that the modified descriptions still appear benign to both LLMs and users. Existing IPI attacks, however, struggle to achieve both high attack success and low detectability in this setting. To address this challenge, we propose GRAFT, an LLM-based optimization method for crafting adversarial tool descriptions. Specifically, GRAFT uses a masking mechanism to identify argument-relevant token positions for targeted injection. It then iteratively refines candidate descriptions using dynamic mutation strategies proposed by an LLM, guided by the agent's tool choices and generated arguments. We evaluate GRAFT on three public datasets against several attack baselines. The results show that GRAFT achieves higher attack success while maintaining low detection rates across five filter-based defenses. It also bypasses several existing IPI defenses. Even under an adaptive defense trained on GRAFT-generated injections, GRAFT remains more effective than the baselines.
tldr: GRAFT is an LLM-based optimization method that crafts adversarial tool descriptions to poison MCP tool metadata, inducing malicious argument generation in LLM agents while evading detection.
motivation: Third-party MCP servers introduce a new attack surface through tool descriptions, but existing indirect prompt injection attacks struggle to combine high attack success with low detectability in this setting.
method: GRAFT uses a masking mechanism to locate argument-relevant token positions for targeted injection and iteratively refines candidate descriptions via LLM-proposed dynamic mutations guided by the agent's tool choices and generated arguments.
result: Across three public datasets, GRAFT achieves higher attack success and lower detection rates than baselines against five filter-based defenses, bypasses several existing IPI defenses, and remains more effective even under an adaptive defense trained on its own outputs.
conclusion: Manipulating tool metadata is a practical and stealthy attack vector for LLM agents, and optimization-based description crafting can evade both static and adaptive defenses.

title: Enhancing Metaverse Security Using Explainable AI-based Intrusion Detection Framework
authors: Esha Kuppanda, Shalaka Mahadik, Pranav M. Pawar, Mithun Mukherjee, Raja Muthalagu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.
tldr: This paper proposes an explainable-AI-based intrusion detection framework that combines classical machine learning models with SHAP and LIME to secure Metaverse-of-Things networks.
motivation: The Metaverse of Things integrates ML and IoT but introduces privacy and security risks, and conventional intrusion detection systems handle high-dimensional data poorly and lack interpretability.
method: The authors benchmark several ML classifiers on three security datasets (ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, BoT-IoT) and apply XAI techniques (SHAP, LIME) to identify the most influential features and select an optimal model.
result: The XGBoost model reached 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023, while Random Forest and Extra Trees achieved 99.99% on BoT-IoT, with SHAP and LIME improving feature relevance and interpretability.
conclusion: An ML-plus-XAI intrusion detection framework can effectively and interpretably safeguard Metaverse-of-Things networks against recent cyberthreats.

title: Suspected Until Inspected: Neuro-Symbolic Detection Of Broken Access Control In Server-Side Web Applications
authors: Chengyao Yang, Zifeng Kang, Dongqi Han, Shihong Zou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Broken access control (BAC) has topped the OWASP Top 10 since 2021. Unfortunately, a decade of detectors still leaves a gap on every front. Static analyzers are tied to one language or framework, dynamic testers cover only the endpoints they manage to exercise, and LLM-based auditors leave the final verdict to an error-prone model. In this paper, we design and implement FLINT, a neuro-symbolic framework that detects BAC in server-side web applications without language- or framework-specific rules. Our key insight is to separate the proposal from the verdict -- an LLM may flag any data access as needing a guard, but only a symbolically verified check can clear it. The neural component enumerates every endpoint and distills each, via demand-driven code slicing, into an authorization certificate whose claims are all grounded in cited code. The symbolic component verifies each claimed check through origin tracing and a lattice-based interprocedural dataflow analysis, so that no access is cleared on the model's word. When applied to popular real-world open-source applications, including Gitea, Grafana, and Strapi, FLINT detected 112 zero-day, exploitable BAC vulnerabilities, 30 of them in projects with over 20,000 GitHub stars. We have responsibly disclosed all of them to the developers. Mattermost, for example, has already confirmed our report and is assigning a CVE identifier.
tldr: FLINT is a neuro-symbolic framework that combines LLM-based endpoint enumeration and code slicing with lattice-based interprocedural dataflow verification to detect broken access control vulnerabilities in server-side web applications.
motivation: Broken access control has topped the OWASP Top 10 since 2021, yet existing static analyzers are language/framework-specific, dynamic testers cover only exercised endpoints, and LLM auditors delegate final verdicts to an error-prone model.
method: The neural component enumerates every endpoint and distills each into an authorization certificate with claims grounded in cited code via demand-driven slicing; the symbolic component then verifies each claimed guard through origin tracing and lattice-based interprocedural dataflow analysis, so no access is cleared on the model's word alone.
result: Applied to real-world open-source applications including Gitea, Grafana, and Strapi, FLINT found 112 zero-day exploitable BAC vulnerabilities, 30 of them in projects with over 20,000 GitHub stars, all responsibly disclosed; Mattermost confirmed the report and is assigning a CVE.
conclusion: Separating vulnerability proposal from verdict enables language-agnostic, symbolically grounded detection of broken access control at scale in production web software.

title: Poisoning Attacks And Collaborative Defense Framework For LightRAG-Based Construction Regulation Knowledge
authors: Yingyan He
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used in construction, yet the security of building-regulation knowledge bases has received little study. This thesis reports a pre-registered experiment on one fully instrumented LightRAG system built on the UK Approved Documents. Using a 150-item benchmark labeled with safety consequences and tampering directions, it evaluates four attacks (text layer, graph layer, fabricated amendment narrative and a defense-aware adaptive attacker) together with a three-layer retrieval-graph-generation defense in a full factorial design. Text-level poisoning succeeded, with success rising with the budget; graph-level poisoning was less effective, contrary to the registered hypothesis. The full defense met the registered criterion and six of the seven configurations met its threshold, but those containing the generation layer did so by refusing 69-80 percent of poisoned queries, costing up to 74 points of clean accuracy, whereas provenance-based retrieval filtering cost no measurable clean accuracy in the configuration used. A second experimental batch showed that excluding a legitimate unregistered amendment caused no measurable loss of accuracy either, as its wording reached the generator through the graph's entity and relationship descriptions, the route the poison took, which no layer inspects. Interactions were strong, so no layer's contribution can be isolated. A reported zero attack success rate is not evidence of detection unless the refusal rate is reported with it: zero arises either because provenance filtering removes every document outside the manifest without judging its content, or because the system refuses. Layered defenses must therefore be evaluated factorially, and regulatory RAG assistants require corpus admission control and version-aware verification before they can support safety-critical decisions.
tldr: A pre-registered factorial study of poisoning attacks and layered defenses on a LightRAG system built over UK building-regulation documents.
motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation is increasingly deployed for safety-critical regulatory advice, yet the security of such knowledge bases—particularly graph-structured RAG—has received little systematic study.
method: Four attacks (text-layer, graph-layer, fabricated amendment narrative, defense-aware adaptive attacker) are tested against a three-layer retrieval-graph-generation defense in a full factorial design using a 150-item benchmark labeled by safety consequence and tampering direction.
result: Text-level poisoning succeeded with success scaling in budget while graph-level poisoning underperformed the registered hypothesis; generation-layer defenses reached thresholds largely by refusing 69–80% of poisoned queries at a cost of up to 74 points of clean accuracy, whereas provenance-based retrieval filtering incurred no measurable clean-accuracy loss.
conclusion: Layered defenses must be evaluated factorially and zero attack success must be reported alongside refusal rates; regulatory RAG assistants need corpus admission control and version-aware verification before supporting safety-critical decisions.

title: Too Fast To Doubt? Skipping Reasoning Leaves Jev-like Models Vulnerable
authors: Yue Li, Hao Wu, Zenan Fu, Xiao Li, Fengyuan Xu, Sheng Zhong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast decision models offer low-latency actions and explicit confidence estimates. We audit four state-of-the-art decision models on 1,440 paired synthetic browser tasks, injecting false conclusions or evidence interpretations through external comments. Across models, clean accuracy averages 91.0%, yet two-shot attack success reaches 81.2%. Mean expected calibration error rises from 2.6% on clean inputs to 36.7% under conclusion poisoning and 36.1% under evidence poisoning. Clean accuracy and calibration therefore do not ensure reliable decisions under injection. We further compare GPT-6 Luna and Luna Decisions, which share the same base model, on 48 matched tasks. With a chain of thought averaging fewer than 30 reasoning tokens per response, low-effort GPT-6 Luna answers 95.83% of poisoned inputs correctly, versus 38.54% for native Luna Decisions, while mean selected-generation latency increases from 0.29 to 1.94 seconds. These results expose a sharp latency-robustness trade-off: skipping reasoning for sub-second speed leaves fast decision models substantially more vulnerable to deceptive web content.
tldr: The paper audits fast decision models (LLM-based agents) on synthetic browser tasks and shows that skipping chain-of-thought reasoning makes them highly vulnerable to injected false conclusions, despite good clean accuracy and calibration.
motivation: Low-latency decision models advertise fast, well-calibrated actions, but it is unclear whether such clean-input performance and confidence estimates translate into robustness against adversarial or deceptive content encountered in real web environments.
method: 1,440 paired synthetic browser tasks were used to inject false conclusions or misinterpreted evidence via external comments (two-shot attacks), measuring accuracy, attack success rate and expected calibration error across four state-of-the-art decision models; additionally GPT-6 Luna and Luna Decisions were compared on 48 matched tasks with varying reasoning-token budgets.
result: Clean accuracy averaged 91.0% and ECE 2.6%, yet two-shot attack success reached 81.2% with ECE rising to ~36% under conclusion or evidence poisoning; enabling fewer than 30 reasoning tokens raised poisoned-input accuracy from 38.54% to 95.83% at a latency cost of 0.29 s to 1.94 s.
conclusion: There is a sharp latency-robustness trade-off: sub-second decision models that skip reasoning are substantially more vulnerable to deceptive injected content, so clean accuracy and calibration are insufficient reliability indicators.

title: To Own Or Not To Own? Endogenous Ownership In Peer-to-Peer Sharing Of Private Autonomous Vehicles
authors: Gioele Zardini Xinling Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous driving allows private owners to release their vehicles to an on-demand platform and earn income when they do not need them. This possibility changes vehicle acquisition incentives, as rental income can encourage purchases, while access to shared vehicles can reduce the need for personal ownership. Understanding these competing effects is essential to assessing the ownership implications of private AVs sharing. While existing models of private AV sharing often take ownership as given, in this paper, we develop a stationary equilibrium model in which vehicle ownership and listing decisions determine service availability and operational frictions, which in turn shape individuals' incentives to own and share. Based on the model, we first characterize individual choices by comparing payoffs of being an owner and a non-owner. We then analyze the resulting potential population partitions, establish conditions for the existence of an active sharing market, and categorize them by owner types. The equilibrium is presented by a system of equations and solved through a tailored algorithm. An illustrative numerical study on calibrated U.S. travel and vehicle cost data shows that sharing can either increase or decrease ownership, depending on the balance between purchases encouraged by rental income and ownership displaced by shared vehicles. The balance is shaped by market parameters, including market density, AV cost, and platform operating conditions. Platform pricing and municipal regulation can also influence ownership through their effects on acquisition incentives and the shared service that makes nonownership attractive. These findings highlight the range of possible ownership outcomes in private AV sharing markets, and the model provides a framework for evaluating how market conditions, platform decisions, and regulation shape these outcomes.
tldr: Develops a stationary equilibrium model of endogenous vehicle ownership and peer-to-peer listing decisions in private autonomous vehicle sharing markets.
motivation: Private AV owners can rent out idle vehicles, which may either encourage additional purchases through rental income or reduce ownership demand via shared access; existing models typically assume ownership exogenously, leaving these competing effects unexamined.
method: A stationary equilibrium model in which ownership and listing decisions jointly determine service availability and operational frictions, characterized via payoff comparisons between owners and non-owners, population partition analysis, and a tailored numerical algorithm on calibrated U.S. travel and vehicle cost data.
result: Sharing can either increase or decrease ownership depending on the balance between rental-income-induced purchases and displaced ownership, with the balance governed by market density, AV cost, platform operating conditions, pricing, and municipal regulation.
conclusion: The framework characterizes the range of possible ownership outcomes and offers a tool for evaluating how market conditions, platform decisions, and regulation shape private AV sharing markets.

title: BinXSight: Fast Binary Program Summarization Via Hierarchical Modular Decomposition
authors: Zhijie Liu, Zhipeng Xue, Zhipeng Gao, Pengfei Jing, Zixiong Qin, Sen Nie, Shi Wu, Liang Feng Zhang, Yutian Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Binary code summarization (BCS) is crucial in fields such as cybersecurity. Particularly, program-level BCS can quickly provide a comprehensive overview of an entire stripped binary without in-depth manual reverse engineering. However, a binary often contains numerous functions with complex interactions, making it challenging to extract its functionality efficiently. Moreover, existing methods focus solely on function-level without considering contextual information, limiting their applicability to program-level analysis. Towards comprehensive and fast program-level BCS, we propose BinXSight, an LLM-powered framework based on hierarchical modular decomposition. Specifically, we first propose binary graph, a new data structure composed of four graphs, to comprehensively represent a binary. Then, based on the binary graph, we hierarchically decompose functions into modules and select the most significant ones. Finally, BinXSight generates a program-level summary from these module summaries. We evaluate BinXSight on stripped binaries across various sizes, fields, platforms, and architectures. Results show that BinXSight outperforms baselines by 23.18% to 46.99%, and summarizes a binary with about 3K functions in 24.3 seconds on average. In addition, a user study with 27 experts shows that BinXSight's high-quality summaries help users quickly understand the whole binary. Our case analysis on recent real-world malware further demonstrates its practical utility.
tldr: BinXSight is an LLM-powered framework that hierarchically decomposes stripped binaries into modules to produce fast, program-level code summaries for cybersecurity analysis.
motivation: Program-level binary code summarization is valuable for reverse engineering and malware analysis, but existing methods work only at the function level and ignore inter-function context, making whole-binary comprehension slow and incomplete.
method: The authors introduce a 'binary graph' data structure combining four graphs to represent a binary, then hierarchically decompose functions into modules, select the most significant modules, and use an LLM to generate module-level summaries that are aggregated into a program-level summary.
result: BinXSight outperforms baselines by 23.18%–46.99% across binaries of varying size, domain, platform, and architecture, summarizing a binary with ~3K functions in about 24.3 seconds on average, with a 27-expert user study and malware case studies confirming practical utility.
conclusion: Hierarchical modular decomposition with LLMs enables scalable, high-quality program-level binary summarization, offering a practical tool for security analysts.

title: Who Grades The Agent? Privilege Separation For Coding-Agent Benchmarks
authors: Nathan Nour Houlamy, Mattia Favretto, Earlence Fernandes, Mauro Conti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed. Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.
tldr: SplitBench is a privilege-separation framework for evaluating AI coding agents that isolates test execution from judging, preventing agents from forging passing scores by tampering with their evaluation infrastructure.
motivation: Coding-agent benchmarks are gamed because grading requires running agent-produced code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process (as demonstrated by BenchJack and a Hugging Face incident); a secure-systems approach is needed to make scores trustworthy.
method: Building on secure systems design principles, the authors separate the execution of task tests from the judgment of results, keeping expected answers in a trusted grader; they port Terminal-Bench and DeepSWE tasks to this framework and attack the converted tasks with adversarial agents that can read grading code but not the answers.
result: 180 of 202 tasks converted successfully, with SplitBench agreeing with native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts and blocking 75% of worst-case adversarial attempts, with remaining exploits traced mostly to weaknesses in original task tests.
conclusion: Privilege separation provides a practical, low-overhead path to robust coding-agent benchmarking, though underlying task designs still need hardening.

title: DNN-Assisted Deterministic Policy Learning For Adaptive Irs-noma-owc Networks
authors: Ahrar N. Hamad, Ahmad A. Qidan, Taisir E. H. El-Gorashi, Jaafar M. H. Elmirghani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) has been considered a promising technology in optical wireless communication (OWC) networks due to its potential to overcome the line-of-sight (LoS) blockage issue and enhance coverage. In this paper, a dynamic IRS-assisted indoor non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-OWC network is modeled, and an optimization problem is formulated to maximize the sum rate subject to the quality-of-service (QoS) requirements of multiple mobile users, by jointly optimizing the power allocation and the IRS mirror orientations, from which the user's decoding order is induced rather than being fixed. Since the problem is non-convex and the channel conditions vary with user mobility, conventional optimization methods may incur considerable computational overhead. Therefore, a two-stage deep neural network-deep reinforcement learning (DNN-DRL) framework is proposed. In the first stage, the DNN estimates the user's positions and orientations in real time, removing the need for perfect knowledge of the user state. In the second stage, a deterministic policy gradient (DPG)-based DRL algorithm uses these estimates to jointly optimize the power allocation and IRS mirror orientations, with the decoding order updated according to the resulting effective channel gains. The results show that the proposed framework approaches the performance upper bounds and outperforms standard DRL algorithms, conventional optimization methods, and deployments without IRS in terms of sum rate and fairness, while achieving faster convergence. Furthermore, online adaptation of the decoding order maintains higher QoS satisfaction than a fixed decoding order, particularly under high user mobility.
tldr: This paper proposes a DNN-DRL framework for jointly optimizing power allocation and IRS mirror orientations in an indoor NOMA-OWC network with mobile users.
motivation: IRS technology can mitigate line-of-sight blockage and improve coverage in optical wireless communication networks, but dynamic user mobility and non-convex optimization make real-time resource allocation challenging.
method: The authors formulate a sum-rate maximization problem under QoS constraints and solve it via a two-stage DNN-DRL approach: a DNN estimates user positions/orientations, and a deterministic policy gradient DRL algorithm optimizes power allocation and IRS orientations while updating the decoding order.
result: The proposed framework approaches performance upper bounds and outperforms standard DRL, conventional optimization, and no-IRS deployments in sum rate and fairness, with faster convergence and better QoS under high mobility.
conclusion: DNN-assisted deterministic policy learning is effective for adaptive IRS-NOMA-OWC networks, and online decoding-order adaptation improves QoS satisfaction especially under user mobility.

title: Source Conditions And Sharp Transition Asymptotics For The Factorization Method With Far-Field Data
authors: Koung Hee Leem George Pelekanos
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The factorization method characterizes an obstacle through a range test, but practical implementations replace the associated Picard series by a regularized approximation. This paper studies the resulting regularization bias for inverse acoustic scattering by impedance obstacles. For a disc, we show that every positive-order H\"older source condition fails at each noncentral interior sampling point, whereas logarithmic source conditions hold uniformly on compact interior subsets for every exponent, with explicit constants. At the center, the bias decays linearly with the regularization parameter. We then derive sharp spectral transition asymptotics through the Lambert W function. These asymptotics determine the stabilization rate inside the obstacle, the iterated-logarithmic growth at the boundary, and the divergence outside. They also yield a threshold rule for which the reconstructed disc converges in measure, together with quantitative boundary-location estimates. For general impedance obstacles, we reduce the spectral decay of the symmetrized far-field operator to that of the data-to-pattern operator and obtain two-sided transition bounds in terms of the inradius and any radius larger than the circumradius. For a simply connected obstacle with analytic boundary, positive analytic impedance, and conformal center inside the obstacle, a Faber--Vekua normal form gives the sharp spectral law in terms of logarithmic capacity, with the same leading constant as for the disc. This class includes every convex analytic obstacle. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted spectral transition and illustrate its use in choosing the regularization level. The analytic normal-form result is proved only for a single boundary component.
tldr: The paper analyzes regularization bias and sharp spectral transition asymptotics for the factorization method in inverse acoustic scattering with far-field data.
motivation: Practical implementations of the factorization method replace the Picard series with a regularized approximation, so understanding the resulting bias and spectral behavior is important for obstacle reconstruction.
method: The authors study source conditions for impedance obstacles, derive spectral transition asymptotics via the Lambert W function, and use Faber-Vekua normal forms for analytic obstacles.
result: They show Holder source conditions fail at noncentral interior points while logarithmic conditions hold, obtain sharp transition bounds, and provide a threshold rule for convergence in measure and boundary-location estimates.
conclusion: The work gives quantitative asymptotics for regularization bias in the factorization method and supports choosing the regularization level, with numerical experiments confirming the predicted spectral transition.

title: From Data Pencils To Image Representations Of Continuous-time Lti Systems
authors: Timo Reis, Philipp Schmitz, Karl Worthmann
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The continuous-time fundamental lemma describes the set of all trajectories of a linear time-invariant system by a Gramian matrix built from measured input--output data and their derivatives. The jet of a trajectory is represented as the Gramian applied to a nonunique parameter satisfying a differential-algebraic equation. We determine the complete Kronecker structure of the associated data pencil for multiple-input multiple-output systems. This enables the construction of a polynomial image representation of the input--output behavior directly from the data. The resulting image matrix has column degrees equal to the controllability indices, and its latent variable is free and serves as a flat output of the system. The computation relies on an orthogonal staircase reduction followed by basis reconstruction using polynomial kernels. We also propose a structure-preserving preconditioning of the Gramian to improve its condition number and facilitate rank decisions in the reduction. We illustrate our approach on a chain of mass-spring-damper systems.
tldr: The paper develops a data-driven image representation for continuous-time linear time-invariant systems using the fundamental lemma and Kronecker structure of data pencils.
motivation: The continuous-time fundamental lemma represents trajectories via a Gramian built from measured input-output data and derivatives, but constructing a polynomial image representation directly from data is nontrivial.
method: The authors determine the complete Kronecker structure of the associated data pencil for MIMO systems and use an orthogonal staircase reduction followed by basis reconstruction via polynomial kernels, with structure-preserving preconditioning.
result: They obtain an image matrix whose column degrees equal the controllability indices, with a free latent variable serving as a flat output, and illustrate the approach on a mass-spring-damper chain.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic data-based polynomial image representation for continuous-time LTI systems and improves numerical rank decisions through preconditioning.

title: Constraint-Aware Anticlustering Decomposition For Certifying Pairwise-Constrained Clustering
authors: Anna Livia Croella, Veronica Piccialli, Antonio M. Sudoso
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Certifying the quality of feasible solutions to large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints remains challenging, as it requires strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value. We propose a decomposition framework that partitions the data points into smaller subsets, called anticlusters, and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), which assigns each connected component of the constraint graph to a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and develop a variable neighborhood search heuristic to construct high-quality decompositions. The resulting lower bound remains valid even when the induced subproblems are not solved to global optimality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets with up to approximately 4,000 observations show that our approach can achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at a modest computational cost.
tldr: The paper proposes a decomposition framework based on a constrained anticlustering problem to compute certified lower bounds and optimality gaps for large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with must-link and cannot-link constraints.
motivation: Certifying solution quality for large-scale constrained minimum sum-of-squares clustering is hard because strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value are difficult to obtain.
method: Data points are partitioned into anticlusters while preserving pairwise constraints via the Constrained Anticlustering Problem, formulated as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and solved heuristically with variable neighborhood search; the induced subproblems yield valid lower bounds even without global optimality.
result: Experiments on synthetic and real datasets with up to roughly 4,000 observations achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at modest computational cost.
conclusion: Constraint-aware anticlustering decomposition offers an effective and computationally affordable route to certifying pairwise-constrained clustering solutions.

title: A Unified Framework For Intelligent Cyber Attack Detection And Alert Correlation
authors: Miguel Silva, Jo\~ao Vitorino, Daniela Pinto, Eva Maia, Ivone Amorim, Isabel Pra\c{c}a
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Security Operations Center (SOC) plays a critical role in detecting, correlating, and responding to modern cyber threats. However, SOCs continue to face challenges related to alert overload, fragmented detection capabilities, and limited collaboration between analysts and automated systems. These issues often result in delayed incident response, analyst fatigue, and an increased risk of overlooking sophisticated, multi-stage attacks that unfold gradually across different layers of the network. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a unified framework for network traffic classification and alert correlation through the use of signature rules, machine learning, and sequential pattern mining algorithms. The solution was evaluated in a controlled testbed environment emulating realistic, multi-stage attack scenarios, including malware exploitation, lateral movement, reconnaissance, and data exfiltration. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in detecting and correlating complex attack behaviors, while providing analysts with actionable insights in line with a human-in-the-loop approach to SOC operations.
tldr: The paper proposes a unified SOC framework that combines signature rules, machine learning, and sequential pattern mining to classify network traffic and correlate alerts for detecting multi-stage cyber attacks.
motivation: Security Operations Centers suffer from alert overload, fragmented detection tools, and limited analyst-automation collaboration, which delays incident response and lets sophisticated multi-stage attacks go unnoticed.
method: The authors integrate signature-based detection, ML-based traffic classification, and sequential pattern mining for alert correlation, evaluated in a controlled testbed emulating malware exploitation, lateral movement, reconnaissance, and data exfiltration.
result: The framework effectively detects and correlates complex multi-stage attack behaviors while providing actionable, human-in-the-loop insights to analysts.
conclusion: A hybrid detection-and-correlation pipeline can reduce SOC alert fatigue and improve detection of gradual, multi-layer attacks within realistic emulated environments.

title: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost Of Protected DeFi Lending
authors: Tarun Chitra, Manvir Schneider, Nagu Thogiti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \[MATH]N[MATH]M[MATH]\Theta(N)[MATH]\Theta()$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.
tldr: The paper models the capital cost of economically securing decentralized finance (DeFi) lending protocols, treating junior capital (loss-absorbing economic security) as a first-class design constraint alongside cryptographic collateral.
motivation: DeFi protocols secure hundreds of billions in assets, but collateral alone cannot absorb all losses; composability means both the amount and the location of economic protection matter, and current designs (Aave, Morpho-like) may be capital-inefficient.
method: The authors build a formal model of asset-dependent protection (ADP) over composable protocol graphs, derive scaling behavior (e.g., Θ(N) with small constants), and optimize graph designs, applying the model to a set of 2026 DeFi cyber-attacks.
result: Optimized designs achieve practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% relative to designs resembling Aave and Morpho across the analyzed attack scenarios.
conclusion: New lending protocols can substantially improve capital efficiency by explicitly optimizing the placement and amount of junior capital, treating it as a primary design constraint.

title: GeoCloak: Defending Against Geolocation Reasoning In Multimodal Language Models Via Perceptual Image Editing
authors: Haoyang Xu, Christian Iha, Colbren Fujimoto, Yingfei Dong, Rui Ning, Liuwan Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.26987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.
tldr: GeoCloak is a cue-aware perceptual image-editing framework that reduces geolocation leakage from images shared with multimodal LLMs by semantically editing location-revealing visual cues.
motivation: Multimodal large language models can infer fine-grained geographic locations from ordinary images using visual, textual, architectural and environmental cues, creating privacy risks even after GPS metadata is stripped.
method: The framework uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions via object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits that disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving overall scene content.
result: Experiments on street-level image datasets show substantially reduced administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, with perceptual-quality scores closer to the originals than pixel-level perturbation baselines.
conclusion: Cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, though deployment cost, semantic plausibility and adaptive evaluation remain open challenges.

title: Proactive Defense Benchmark Against Deepfake Generation
authors: Joonhyuk Baek, Wonjune Seo, Jae-Yun Kim, Saerom Park, Hoki Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite the proliferation of proactive defenses against deepfakes, the lack of a unified evaluation protocol precludes fair comparison and masks critical vulnerabilities. To bridge this gap, we present the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically assesses disruption, robustness, and transferability encompassing pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics. Our extensive analysis reveals that fidelity and identity metrics capture orthogonal performance axes, often leading to conflicting interpretations when relied upon individually. Furthermore, we identify a fundamental trade-off where peak white-box performance signals overfitting, and we introduce a calibrated evaluation to correct generator-induced identity bias. By exposing these blind spots, we establish a rigorous standard to guide the development of genuinely generalizable protections. Project page is available at: [URL].
tldr: This paper introduces the first comprehensive benchmark for proactive deepfake defenses, evaluating disruption, robustness, and transferability across pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics.
motivation: The proliferation of proactive deepfake defenses lacks a unified evaluation protocol, preventing fair comparison and hiding critical vulnerabilities such as overfitting to white-box attacks and generator-induced identity bias.
method: The authors build a systematic benchmark that assesses protection methods along disruption, robustness, and transferability axes using pixel-level, perceptual, and identity-based metrics, plus a calibrated evaluation to correct identity bias.
result: Fidelity and identity metrics are shown to capture orthogonal performance axes that can yield conflicting interpretations, and peak white-box performance is found to signal overfitting rather than genuine generalizability.
conclusion: The benchmark exposes blind spots in current evaluation practice and establishes a rigorous standard intended to guide development of genuinely generalizable proactive deepfake protections.

title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails And Auditing Spectral Coupling In Open-Weight LLMs
authors: Feng Huang, Qiang Huang, Yue Gao, Mei Zhang, Bin Liu, Lihua Ju, Xinhao Wei, Yongfeng Huang, Yu Qing, Yunqi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.
tldr: The paper introduces Cleave, a training-free weight-editing attack that removes or selectively lifts safety guardrails in open-weight LLMs and proposes spectral coupling audits as a defense.
motivation: Open-weight LLMs are deployed locally without provider control, and existing safety guardrails can potentially be bypassed by malicious users; the authors aim to expose and mitigate this vulnerability.
method: The attack identifies residual writing weights responsible for refusal behavior and directly edits them to remove safety restrictions, optionally targeting only cybersecurity restrictions; defenses combine pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits.
result: Cleave achieves up to 67.97% attack success on seven safety benchmarks across five LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0x on cybersecurity tasks, and the proposed defense achieves 100% detection recall at 1% false-positive rate.
conclusion: Safety guardrails in open-weight LLMs are vulnerable to targeted weight edits, and spectral coupling audits can help detect such tampering, though the work is outside quantum information research.

title: Recognizing $k$-inducible Digraphs Is NP-complete
authors: Fabian Frank Felix Brandt
abstract: ArXiv:2611.27965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A digraph is k-inducible if its arcs correspond to the pairwise majority relation of a preference profile with k voters. By McGarvey's theorem, every asymmetric digraph is k-inducible for some k, but for every fixed k there are digraphs that are not k-inducible. Whether a digraph is 1-inducible or 2-inducible can easily be decided in polynomial time. The complexity of deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible for every fixed [MATH] has been a long-standing open problem. We prove that deciding whether a tournament is 3-inducible is NP-complete and then leverage this result to show that deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible is NP-complete for every fixed [MATH]. Our results imply that, unless P=NP, k-inducible digraphs cannot be characterized by finitely many forbidden induced subdigraphs.
tldr: The paper proves that recognizing k-inducible digraphs, which arise from majority preferences of k voters, is NP-complete for every fixed k ≥ 3.
motivation: The complexity of deciding k-inducibility for fixed k has been a long-standing open problem in social choice theory; earlier cases k = 1,2 are polynomial-time decidable.
method: The authors first prove NP-completeness of deciding whether a tournament is 3-inducible, then reduce this to establish NP-completeness for every fixed k ≥ 3.
result: They show that k-inducible digraph recognition is NP-complete for all fixed k ≥ 3, implying that unless P=NP such digraphs cannot be characterized by finitely many forbidden induced subdigraphs.
conclusion: The results settle the complexity of k-inducibility recognition and rule out finite forbidden-subdigraph characterizations under standard complexity assumptions.
